Backup and restore

Where your progress is saved

Your ticks, logs, scores and applications are saved inside this browser on this computer. They stay when you close the browser, but not if you clear browsing data, switch browsers or move to another computer. A backup file keeps them safe.

Automatic backup file

Keeps a copy of everything in one file on your computer, updated a second or two after every change. Save it in your PM-Training folder. If you ever clear your browser or switch browsers, use Restore from a backup below and choose this file.

Download a backup

Saves everything to one small file in your Downloads folder. With automatic backup on, you only need this for an extra copy; without it, do this every Sunday after your weekly review.

Restore from a backup

Replaces the progress in this browser with the progress in a backup file. Use it after clearing your browser, or to carry on in another browser or on another computer.

Start over

Clears all saved progress in this browser, and in the automatic backup file if it’s on. Download a backup first if you might want it back.

    Program plan

    Overview

    After the 4-week interview sprint (Oct 19 to Nov 15), you’ll train for 14 weeks, from Mon Nov 16, 2026 to Sun Feb 21, 2027, at 31 hours a week (about 440 hours in all). By the end you should work at the level of a mid-level PM and be ready to interview for AI product roles at fintech companies in India, Europe, Singapore or Canada.

    Every skill is practised on a real product: Melange Research (melangeresearch.com), your research site for people in India who invest in mutual funds every month through a SIP. Each week ends with a Melange deliverable that gets graded and goes into your job portfolio.

    The program doesn’t depend on Claude. The schedule, goals, rubric and coach prompts all live in this doc. The prompts work in ChatGPT, Gemini or any other AI chat, and copies of everything are saved on your computer. The last section, Running it with any AI tool, or none, explains how.

    Day-by-day tasks: Daily schedule · Copy-paste prompts for any AI: Coach prompts

    Lessons, cheat sheets for every topic, templates for every deliverable, and a glossary: Product Management Course: Lessons and Cheat Sheets

    To start applying sooner, use the 4-week interview sprint: a separate 4-week course focused on interviews and applications.

    Roadmap

    The interview sprint comes first. Each phase after it ends with a gate deliverable, and job applications run from sprint Week 2 to the end.

    Week-by-week plan

    Each week has one focus and one Melange deliverable, due Sunday. Gate weeks close a phase: the deliverable must score 3 (Mid PM) or higher on the rubric.

    Week Dates Focus Melange deliverable (due Sunday)
    0 Oct 17–18 Setup Baseline: one-paragraph description of Melange, log started
    1 Nov 16–22 The PM role and product thinking Product brief v0 (one page)
    2 Nov 23–29 User research Interview guide + notes from 3 SIP investor interviews
    3 Nov 30–Dec 6 Synthesis and problem framing Insight report (5 interviews) + opportunity solution tree · Gate 1
    4 Dec 7–13 Strategy and competition Teardown of 3 competitors + positioning statement + market sizing
    5 Dec 14–20 Prioritisation and roadmaps RICE-scored backlog + Now/Next/Later roadmap · Gate 2
    6 Dec 21–27 Metrics North-star metric framework + event tracking plan, analytics installed
    7 Dec 28–Jan 3 Data and experiments Experiment brief and results + SQL exercise set · Gate 3
    8 Jan 4–10 Specs and design PRD + wireframes for the top roadmap item
    9 Jan 11–17 Delivery and launch Shipped feature + launch plan + release notes + retro · Gate 4
    10 Jan 18–24 Technical foundations and how AI works Melange system map + AI opportunity memo
    11 Jan 25–31 AI product management AI feature spec + 30-case eval set with results · Gate 5
    12 Feb 1–7 Fintech domain and compliance Compliance review of Melange + compliance-aware feature spec
    13 Feb 8–14 Leadership and the job simulation Quarterly business review memo + simulation debrief
    14 Feb 15–21 Interview readiness Portfolio of 5 case studies + resume + 5 mock interviews · Final gate

    The 4-week interview sprint runs before Week 1, from Oct 19 to Nov 15, so you’ll already be applying. Keep applying throughout, and add each graded deliverable to your portfolio as you go.

    Daily routine

    Each weekday is one fixed 4-hour block. For a trader, right after market close works well (for example, 4:30 to 8:30 pm). Pick your slot and keep it every day.

    Block Time What you do
    1. Drill 30 min One timed interview-style question of the week’s drill type, using the Drill prompt or a question from the course doc’s Question bank
    2. Learn 90 min The day’s Learn topic: read the matching cheat sheet in the course doc, then run a coach session with the Lesson prompt
    3. Build 90 min The day’s Build task on Melange, from the Daily schedule
    4. Log 30 min Write the daily log, tick the day off, and note one decision you made and why

    The drill type changes as the program moves: guesstimates (Weeks 1–3), product sense (4–5), metrics diagnosis (6–7), execution (8–9), AI PM questions (10–11), behavioural stories (12–13), and full mock interviews in Week 14. On Monday, Wednesday and Friday, one more hour follows the Log block: job search (see Job search during the 14 weeks).

    Weekly rhythm

    The week totals 34 hours: 31 of training and 3 of job search. Use the one spare hour (up to 35) for catching up or redoing weak work, never for skipping ahead.

    Day Hours Focus
    Monday to Friday 4 each (20) Drill, learn, build, log
    Monday, Wednesday and Friday 1 each (3) Job search after the Log block: applications, follow-ups and conversations
    Saturday 6 Job simulation (2 h), deliverable work (3 h), time with real SIP investors (1 h)
    Sunday 5 Weekly review and grading (1.25 h), quiz (0.25 h), revise the deliverable (2 h), catch up (1 h), plan next week (0.5 h)
    Total 34 31 training, 3 job search

    How you stay on track

    You stay on track through eight habits. None of them depends on any one AI tool.

    • Daily log (Block 4). Write it on the hub’s Today page, which keeps one entry per day, or in a running notes file, using the template below.
    • Sunday review. Paste the week’s deliverable and logs into the Weekly review prompt. Then record hours, status and grade in the hub’s Weekly log, or in the Progress log below.
    • Phase gates. A gate deliverable needs a grade of 3 or higher. If it scores lower, revise it during the next week’s catch-up hours and get it re-graded before the following Sunday.
    • Off-track triggers. If you log under 25 hours in a week, or miss two days in a row, run the Re-plan prompt on Sunday. Shrink or drop tasks instead of stacking them. If you need more time, the plan can end on Feb 28 instead of Feb 21 (one buffer week).
    • A human check once per phase. Show one deliverable to a working PM, for example through a free mentorship platform like ADPList or a PM community. AI grading is useful, but a real PM will catch different things.
    • Weekly quiz (Sunday, 15 minutes). Run the Quiz me prompt on the week’s lesson and cheat sheet, or answer the lesson’s Check yourself questions without looking. Revisit anything you miss in the next week’s Learn block.
    • Energy check. You also trade full-time. After a draining market day, do the Drill and Log only and move Learn and Build to the catch-up hour. If that happens three times in a week, run the Re-plan prompt. Protect sleep before hours.
    • Keep your work in one place. Save everything you write in that week’s folder under Wayne-App\PM-Training\Work. The hub’s Today page shows which folder, with a button that copies its path. Finished case studies go in Work\Portfolio; resumes, cover letters, prep packs and debriefs go in Work\Job search. Treat AI chats as drafts only.

    Daily log template

    DAILY LOG — [date]
Did:
Learned:
Stuck on:
One decision I made, and why:
Hours:

    Grading rubric

    Score each deliverable from 1 to 4 on five dimensions: problem clarity, user evidence, trade-offs, metrics, and communication. Your grade is the average, rounded down.

    Score Level What the work looks like
    1 Beginner Jumps to solutions, has no user evidence, sets vague goals
    2 Junior PM States a clear problem with some evidence, but applies frameworks mechanically and success isn’t measurable
    3 Mid PM Names a specific segment, uses real evidence, makes trade-offs explicit, defines measurable success, writes clearly
    4 Senior PM Ties the work to business strategy, anticipates risks and second-order effects, and drives a decision in few words

    Job search during the 14 weeks

    The goal is a job, so the search doesn’t stop after the sprint. On Monday, Wednesday and Friday, add one hour of job search after the Log block: 3 hours a week, on top of the 31 hours of training.

    Weekly targets:

    What Target each week
    Tailored applications 5, each with the resume adjusted to the job description
    Conversations with PMs or hiring managers 2, for referrals, advice or introductions
    Follow-ups Every application or message older than 7 days, once
    Tracker Updated every Friday in the hub’s Applications page

    When a real interview comes in:

    1. The same day: build a prep pack with the Company prep pack prompt, and use the company’s product for 30 minutes.
    2. The next one or two days: swap the Build block for mocks of that company’s rounds with the Mock interviewer prompt. Keep the Learn block.
    3. Within an hour after the interview: run the Interview debrief prompt and send a thank-you note.
    4. On Sunday: move the skipped Build tasks into the catch-up hour, or use the buffer week. A real interview always comes before the schedule.

    Read your funnel every Sunday (Lesson 15): if 20 applications bring no replies, fix your targeting, resume and referrals before sending more; if recruiter screens don’t lead to rounds, fix your story; if rounds don’t lead to offers, practise the weakest round type in your scorecard.

    Finding SIP investors to interview

    Weeks 2 and 3 need five interviews, and the rest of the program needs a steady supply of real users. Build the list early.

    • Who: people running at least one SIP for a year who choose their own funds. Ask two screening questions before booking.
    • Where: people who signed up on melangeresearch.com, friends of friends, past colleagues, LinkedIn contacts, and investing communities such as r/IndiaInvestments.
    • How many: send about 8 requests for every 3 interviews. List 15 names by Sat Nov 21.
    • How: use the interview request message and consent script in the Templates tab. Offer a short summary of what you learn as thanks.
    • Privacy: don’t record names or account details in your notes. Number your participants instead.

    Keep a short list of people happy to talk again, so later weeks (usability tests, launch feedback) don’t start from zero.

    How you’ll know it’s working

    • Baseline and exit mocks: on Sun Oct 18, do three timed mock interviews (product sense, metrics, behavioural) with the Mock interview prompt and log the scores in the hub’s scorecard. Repeat the same three on Sun Nov 15 and Sun Feb 21. The difference is your proof of progress.
    • Gates: every gate at 3 (Mid PM) or higher.
    • Scorecard: each core round type averaging 3 or higher over its last three mocks.
    • Job funnel: applications sent, replies, recruiter screens, interview rounds and offers, read every Sunday.
    • Hours: 31 hours of training and 3 of job search each week, logged in the hub.

    Public proof

    Hiring managers trust evidence more than claims, so publish as you go rather than at the end.

    • Portfolio page by Sat Oct 31: one public page (Notion or similar) with the Melange case study, using the portfolio template. Link it from your resume and LinkedIn.
    • A case study after every gate: turn the graded deliverable into a one-page case study with the Case study writer prompt, in that Sunday’s catch-up hour.
    • A LinkedIn post every other Saturday (Nov 28, Dec 12, Dec 26, Jan 9, Jan 23 and Feb 6): one lesson from your Melange work, using the LinkedIn post editor prompt. Never share members’ personal details.

    Resources by phase

    The free resources are enough to complete the program. The books are optional and go deeper.

    Phase Free Optional books
    1. Discovery (Weeks 1–3) Teresa Torres’s Product Talk blog; Lenny’s Podcast episodes on user research The Mom Test (Rob Fitzpatrick); Continuous Discovery Habits (Teresa Torres)
    2. Strategy and prioritisation (4–5) Lenny’s Newsletter free posts; Reforge blog articles Inspired (Marty Cagan); Escaping the Build Trap (Melissa Perri); Obviously Awesome (April Dunford)
    3. Metrics and experiments (6–7) Amplitude’s North Star Playbook; SQLBolt interactive SQL lessons Lean Analytics (Alistair Croll, Benjamin Yoskovitz)
    4. Execution and launch (8–9) Shape Up by Basecamp (free online book); Atlassian’s Agile Coach guides None needed
    5. Technical and AI PM (10–11) Hamel Husain’s blog posts on AI evals; the free prompting guides from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic; Generative AI for Everyone (Andrew Ng, free to audit) AI Engineering (Chip Huyen)
    6. Fintech, leadership and interviews (12–14) sebi.gov.in and rbi.org.in for regulations; the DPDP Act 2023 text; BaFin’s English site; Exponent’s free mock-interview videos on YouTube Cracking the PM Interview (Gayle McDowell, Jackie Bavaro); Decode and Conquer (Lewis Lin)

    Running it with any AI tool, or none

    You can finish the whole program without a Claude subscription. Three things make it portable:

    1. The content is in files you own. The full program and the course doc are saved on your computer in Wayne-App\PM-Training as Word, PDF and Markdown files. The easiest way in is Career Hub (PM-Training-Hub.html; the Career Hub shortcut on your desktop opens it). It works in any browser with no internet or account: it shows today’s tasks, and lets you tick days off, log weekly hours and grades, score mock interviews and track applications. Progress is saved in that browser and, once you turn on automatic backup on the Backup and restore page, to a file in your PM-Training folder after every change. Word and PDF are for reading and printing, and the Markdown files open in free notes apps such as Obsidian or Notion.
    2. The coach is a prompt, not a product. The Coach prompts tab has twelve self-contained prompts. Paste them into ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek or any capable AI chat, fill in the [brackets] from the Daily schedule, and the AI plays the same role: teacher, drill master, stakeholder, grader, interviewer or planner. On the hub’s Today page, Copy prompt fills in the brackets for you.
    3. Grading follows a fixed rubric. Any AI, a mentor or you yourself can score against the same rubric, so grades stay comparable when you switch tools.

    What changes without Claude: this doc can’t be updated by me, comments won’t reach me, and other AI tools won’t remember your earlier sessions. To fix the memory gap, start every new chat by pasting the Context block from the Coach prompts tab plus your latest Progress log.

    If no AI is available at all: answer the drills on paper and self-grade them with the rubric, use the cheat sheets and free resources for each day’s Learn topic, and swap deliverables with a peer or mentor for grading.

    Interview sprint

    Overview

    This sprint gets you ready to interview for product roles in 4 weeks, from Mon Oct 19 to Sun Nov 15, 2026, at the same 31 hours a week. You start applying in Week 2. By the end you’ll have 30 targeted applications out, a PM-style resume, two portfolio case studies, and three full mock interview loops at Mid PM level.

    It’s built like the 14-week program, with less depth. Each day you learn one interview round, practise it out loud against a strict AI interviewer, and spend over an hour on your job search. Every week ends with a graded gate.

    How it fits: do this sprint first, after the Week 0 setup in the Daily schedule tab. The 14-week program follows from Nov 16 to Feb 21 and builds deeper skills while you interview. Keep applying the whole time, and treat your first real interviews as practice too, since each one shows you what to fix.

    Works without Claude: the answer structures, trackers and prompts in this tab work with any AI tool. A copy is also saved on your computer in Wayne-App\PM-Training.

    Model answers and templates: model answers for every round are in cheat sheet 13, practice questions with outlines are in the Question bank tab, and templates for STAR stories, case studies, resume bullets, referral messages and your portfolio page are in the Templates tab, all in Product Management Course: Lessons and Cheat Sheets.

    When a real interview comes in: build a prep pack with the Company prep pack prompt the same day, swap the next Practise block for mocks of that company’s rounds, and run the Interview debrief prompt within an hour of the interview. The Plan tab’s section Job search during the 14 weeks has the full steps.

    Tax deadlines during the sprint: if your trading accounts need a tax audit, the audit report is due Oct 21 and the return (ITR) Nov 21, 2026, the dates as extended by CBDT. Both are in the day plan so the sprint doesn’t crowd them out. (source)

    Roles to target

    Your edge is domain depth: you trade F&O full time, you built your own trading platform, and you run Melange Research, a research site for people who invest through a monthly SIP. Aim where that counts most, and treat senior AI PM roles as stretch applications.

    Priority Role type Why you fit
    1 PM or Associate PM at brokers, trading and investing apps, and wealth-tech You’re their target user, and you’ve built both a trading platform and an investing research site
    2 PM for AI features at fintechs (research, insights, assistants) Melange is a live research product, and your trading platform uses AI for news and sentiment
    3 Product analyst or product operations at a fintech A common route into PM that uses your data and risk skills
    4 Stretch: AI PM or senior PM roles Apply selectively, with a referral where possible

    You’re targeting India, Europe, Singapore and Canada. Outside India, focus on fintechs that hire in English, and check each listing for relocation and visa support. The hub’s Jobs page lists current openings by priority and region.

    Week-by-week plan

    Each week covers a group of interview rounds and ends with a gate you must pass at 3 (Mid PM) or higher.

    Week Dates Focus Deliverables (due Sunday) Gate
    1 Oct 19–25 Your story and the PM interview 90-second intro, 8 STAR stories, PM resume v1, updated LinkedIn, list of 30 target companies Intro and stories graded 3+
    2 Oct 26–Nov 1 Product sense and design Melange case study, 10 scored product sense answers, first 10 applications, 10 referral messages Last 3 product sense mocks average 3+
    3 Nov 2–8 Metrics, execution, estimation and strategy Second case study (your Quicko ITR-3 teardown), one timed take-home, 10 more applications Last 3 metrics mocks average 3+
    4 Nov 9–15 AI PM, fintech, behavioural depth and full loops 3 full mock loops, a prep pack for each company you’re interviewing with, 10 more applications Core round types average 3+

    Diwali (Sun Nov 8) falls in Week 3, so that week is lighter and its review moves to Friday.

    Daily routine

    Weekdays are one 4-hour block. Practise out loud: real interviews are spoken, so use your AI app’s voice mode if it has one, and record yourself on your phone.

    Block Time What you do
    1. Learn 45 min The day’s round: read its answer structure below, then its model answer in cheat sheet 13 of the course doc
    2. Practise 90 min Two timed questions with the Mock interviewer prompt, or two from the course doc’s Question bank, answered out loud
    3. Job search 75 min The day’s job-search task: resume, portfolio, applications or outreach
    4. Review 30 min Rewrite your weakest answer, then update the scorecard and the application tracker

    Saturday (6 hours): a full mock loop of 2–3 rounds back to back (3 h), one mock with a real person (1 h), portfolio work (2 h).

    Sunday (5 hours): weekly review and gate (1.5 h), fix your weakest round (2 h), applications and tracker (1 h), plan next week (0.5 h).

    Answer structures for each round

    Interviewers score how you structure an answer as much as your ideas. Use these as starting points and adapt them to the question.

    Round What they test Structure
    Tell me about yourself Clarity, motivation, fit Present (what you do now) → past (what built your edge) → why product → why this company. 90 seconds
    Product sense: design or improve User empathy, prioritisation, creativity Clarify the goal → pick one user segment → list their pain points → choose one → 3 solutions → pick one and name the trade-off → first version → success metrics → risks
    Metric dropped Calm, structured diagnosis Clarify the metric and time frame → rule out data or tracking errors → internal causes (releases, bugs, pricing) vs external (season, market, competitors, regulation) → segment by platform, region, new vs existing users → find the funnel step → hypothesis → how to confirm → fix and guardrail
    Metrics and goals Knowing what success means Product goal → north-star metric → 2–3 input metrics → guardrail metrics → how you’d measure them
    Estimation Reasoning with numbers Clarify scope → choose top-down or bottom-up → state each assumption with a reason → calculate with round numbers → sanity-check
    Strategy Business judgment Market and customer → company strengths → competition → 2–3 options → recommendation with risks → how you’d test it cheaply
    Execution and trade-offs Getting things shipped Goal → options → criteria (impact, effort, risk, strategic fit) → decision → what you’d watch after launch
    Behavioural (STAR) Ownership, influence, learning Situation (one sentence) → task → your actions (most of the time; say “I”) → result with a number → what you learned
    AI PM Judgment about AI Is AI the right tool? → data needed → approach (prompting, RAG or fine-tuning) → evals → failure modes and guardrails → UX for trust → cost and latency → metrics
    Fintech twist (any round) Domain maturity Add risk, fraud, compliance (SEBI, RBI or BaFin) and user trust to every answer
    Take-home assignment Written thinking One page: problem and user → evidence → options → recommendation → metrics → risks → next steps

    The habit that matters most: before answering, take 30 seconds to plan, say your structure out loud, then begin.

    Day by day

    Week 1 · Oct 19–25 · Your story and the PM interview

    By Sunday you can: tell your story in 90 seconds and explain what each interview round tests.

    Deliverables: 90-second intro, 8 STAR stories, PM resume v1, updated LinkedIn, list of 30 target companies.

    Gate: intro and stories graded 3 or higher.

    Week 2 · Oct 26–Nov 1 · Product sense and design

    By Sunday you can: answer design and improvement questions with a clear structure, for fintech and consumer products.

    Deliverables: Melange case study, 10 scored product sense answers, first 10 applications, 10 referral messages.

    Gate: last 3 product sense mocks average 3 or higher.

    Week 3 · Nov 2–8 · Metrics, execution, estimation and strategy

    By Sunday you can: diagnose a metric drop, set goals, make trade-offs, and reason about strategy under time pressure.

    Deliverables: second case study (your Quicko ITR-3 teardown), one timed take-home, 10 more applications.

    Gate: last 3 metrics mocks average 3 or higher.

    Diwali falls on Sun Nov 8, so this week is lighter (about 21 hours) and the review moves to Friday.

    Week 4 · Nov 9–15 · AI PM, fintech, behavioural depth and full loops

    By Sunday you can: handle AI and fintech questions, tell strong stories under pressure, and pass full interview loops.

    Deliverables: 3 full mock loops, a prep pack for each company you’re interviewing with, 10 more applications (30 in total).

    Gate (final): the core rounds (product sense, metrics, estimation, strategy, behavioural and AI PM) each average 3 or higher in the scorecard.

    Interview prompts for any AI tool

    Start each new chat with the Sprint context block, then paste the prompt you need and fill in the [brackets].

    Sprint context (paste first in every new chat)

    SPRINT CONTEXT
I'm preparing for product manager interviews over 4 weeks. Background: full-time F&O trader in India with no formal PM experience. I run Melange Research (melangeresearch.com), a research site for people in India who invest in mutual funds every month through a SIP: free charts of the economy and markets, and for research-preview members, models tested on past Indian market data after costs and tax, with one plain-language answer each month on whether that month's SIP goes into shares, gold or a mix. I also built my own trading platform, with market-regime analysis, behavioural checks that block impulsive trades, real-time options pricing, AI news and sentiment analysis, and an Android app.

Target roles: PM or Associate PM at brokers, trading and investing apps and fintechs; PM for AI features; or product analyst. Locations: India, Europe, Singapore or Canada.

Scoring: 1-4 on structure, insight, user focus, metrics and communication. 1 = Beginner, 2 = Junior PM, 3 = Mid PM (hireable), 4 = Senior PM.

Current week: [week and focus]
My scorecard so far: [paste]

    Mock interviewer (daily)

    MOCK INTERVIEWER
Act as a strict PM interviewer at a [type of company] in [India / Europe / Singapore / Canada], hiring for [role]. Round: [tell me about yourself / product sense / metrics / estimation / strategy / execution / behavioural / AI PM / fintech].

Ask one question at a time and wait for my answer. Push with realistic follow-ups, interrupt me if I ramble, and don't help me.

After each answer, score it 1-4 on structure, insight, user focus, metrics and communication. Give my 2 biggest fixes, then show a strong answer outline.

After [2] questions, give an overall hire or no-hire for this round.

    Story builder (Week 1)

    STORY BUILDER
Help me build a STAR story for interviews from this experience: [describe it in a few lines].

Ask me questions until you have the situation, my specific actions and a measurable result. Then write it as a 2-minute spoken answer in my voice, and list 5 interview questions this story can answer.

    Resume review (Week 1, then per role)

    RESUME REVIEW
Act as a hiring manager for [role] at a fintech.
My resume: [paste]
The job description: [paste]

I'm moving from full-time trading into product management. Tell me what stands out and what's missing in a 10-second scan. Rewrite each bullet to show impact with numbers, in product language, without overstating my experience. List the 5 keywords from the job description my resume should include.

    Recruiter screen

    RECRUITER SCREEN
Act as a recruiter running a 20-minute screening call for [role] at [type of company] in [India / Europe / Singapore / Canada]. Ask about my background, why I'm moving into product, why this company, salary expectations, notice period and work authorisation, the way a real recruiter would.

At the end, tell me whether I'd pass to the next round and what to say differently.

    Company prep pack (once you have an interview)

    COMPANY PREP PACK
Job description: [paste]
What I know about the company: [paste notes from its website, app and recent news]

Build a one-page prep pack: what the role needs most, the 8 questions I'm most likely to get, which of my stories fits each, 3 product ideas for their app with success metrics, and 5 sharp questions to ask the interviewer.

    Answer upgrade (Review block)

    ANSWER UPGRADE
Question: [paste]
My answer: [paste]

Rewrite my answer the way a Senior PM would answer it in an interview, keeping my own examples. Show the structure you used and list the 3 changes that matter most.

    Sprint weekly review (Sundays)

    SPRINT WEEKLY REVIEW
Act as a hiring manager reviewing my interview preparation.
Week: [number]
This week's gate: [paste from the plan]
My scorecard: [paste]
My application tracker: [paste]
Hours this week: [number]

1. Which round types are ready (average 3+), and which aren't?
2. Did I pass this week's gate? If not, what exactly must improve?
3. What are my 3 biggest weaknesses, with one drill for each?
4. Am I on pace for 30 applications by the end of Week 4?
5. Set my practice priorities for next week.

    Interview debrief (after every real interview)

    INTERVIEW DEBRIEF
I just had an interview.
Company and role: [ ]
Round: [recruiter screen / hiring manager / product sense / metrics / strategy / behavioural / AI PM / case]
Questions they asked, as close to word for word as I remember: [paste]
My answers, briefly: [paste]
How it felt, and anything they said about next steps: [ ]

1. Score each answer 1-4 against the rubric, with one line of evidence.
2. What did the interviewer most likely want to learn from each question?
3. My 3 biggest gaps, with one drill for each before the next round.
4. Questions to prepare for the next round at this company.
5. A short thank-you note I can send today.

    Offer negotiation (once you have an offer)

    OFFER NEGOTIATION
Play a recruiter who has just made me an offer for [role] at [company] in [India / Europe / Singapore / Canada].
The offer: [base pay, bonus, joining date, other terms]
What I know about the market range: [paste your research]
What matters most to me: [ ]

Negotiate realistically: push back, mention budget limits, and test whether I hold my ground. When I type END, give feedback on what I gave away, what I could have asked for, and the exact words to use in the real call.

    German CV and cover letter (for roles in Germany)

    GERMAN CV
Convert my resume into a German-style CV (Lebenslauf) and a one-page cover letter (Anschreiben) in English for [role] at [company] in Germany.
My resume: [paste]
The job description: [paste]

For the CV: newest first, month and year for every role, one to two pages, no photo, impact bullets. For the cover letter: why this company, my two or three most relevant achievements, my availability and work-permit situation in one line, and a polite close. Then list anything a German recruiter would expect that's missing from my resume.

    Free resources

    • Your own recordings. Watching yourself back is the fastest way to cut filler words and rambling.
    • Exponent’s free mock-interview videos on YouTube. Watch one per round type before you practise it.
    • ADPList. Free sessions with working PMs, useful for the weekly human mock.
    • Lenny’s Newsletter and Podcast. Free posts and episodes on PM interviews and moving into product.
    • Optional books: Cracking the PM Interview (Gayle McDowell, Jackie Bavaro) and Decode and Conquer (Lewis Lin).

    Week 1 · Nov 16–22 · The PM role and product thinking

    Phase 2 · Strategy and prioritisation

    Week 4 · Dec 7–13 · Strategy and competition

    By Sunday you can: analyse competitors, write a positioning statement, and size a market.

    Week 5 · Dec 14–20 · Prioritisation and roadmaps · Gate 2

    By Sunday you can: prioritise with RICE and opportunity cost, say no with reasons, and build an outcome-based roadmap.

    Deliverable: RICE-scored backlog + Now/Next/Later roadmap. Gate 2.

    Phase 3 · Metrics and experiments

    Week 6 · Dec 21–27 · Metrics

    By Sunday you can: define a north-star metric and its inputs, map a funnel, and write a tracking plan.

    Week 7 · Dec 28–Jan 3 · Data and experiments · Gate 3

    By Sunday you can: write basic SQL, design an A/B test, and diagnose a metric drop step by step.

    Deliverable: experiment brief with results (or a test plan, if traffic is too low) + SQL exercise set. Gate 3.

    Drill: one metrics question a day.

    Phase 4 · Execution and launch

    Week 8 · Jan 4–10 · Specs and design

    By Sunday you can: write a PRD engineers can build from, and sketch wireframes.

    Deliverable: shipped feature + launch plan + release notes + retro. Gate 4.

    Add your Phase 1–4 work to your resume and applications this week.

    Phase 5 · Technical and AI PM

    Week 10 · Jan 18–24 · Technical foundations and how AI works

    By Sunday you can: explain Melange’s architecture and data flow, and how LLMs, RAG and agents work.

    Deliverable: Melange system map + AI opportunity memo.

    Week 12 · Feb 1–7 · Fintech domain and compliance

    By Sunday you can: explain the main Indian and German rules that shape fintech products, and work with compliance as a PM.

    Coach prompts

    These twelve prompts work in any AI chat tool, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and DeepSeek. Start each new chat with the Context block, then paste the prompt you need and fill in the [brackets] from the Daily schedule, or use Copy prompt on the hub’s Today page, which fills them in for you.     0. Context block (paste first in every new chat)

    CONTEXT
I am training to become a product manager. Background: I am a full-time F&O trader in India with no formal PM experience. Goal: an AI product manager role at a fintech company in India, Europe, Singapore or Canada. I'm also open to roles where my trading experience is the edge, such as derivatives or trading specialist roles.

Program: a 14-week PM training program (Nov 16, 2026 to Feb 21, 2027) that follows a 4-week interview sprint, about 31 hours a week. Phases: 1 Discovery, 2 Strategy and prioritisation, 3 Metrics and experiments, 4 Execution and launch, 5 Technical and AI PM, 6 Fintech, leadership and interviews.

Practice product: Melange Research (melangeresearch.com), my own research site for people in India who invest in mutual funds every month through a SIP. Anyone can read free charts of India's and the world's economy and markets. Research-preview members get research models tested on past Indian market data after costs and tax, ranked for their monthly amount and years, and one plain-language answer each month on whether that month's SIP goes into shares, gold or a mix. Its users are SIP investors, not traders. It says it is general research, not investment advice.

Grading rubric: score 1-4 on each of problem clarity, user evidence, trade-offs, metrics and communication. 1 = Beginner (jumps to solutions, no evidence). 2 = Junior PM (clear problem, some evidence, frameworks applied mechanically). 3 = Mid PM (specific segment, real evidence, explicit trade-offs, measurable success). 4 = Senior PM (tied to strategy, anticipates risks, drives a decision concisely). Grade = average, rounded down.

Current week: [week number and focus]
My latest progress log: [paste]

    • Save the best explanations into your notes file. Over 14 weeks, your notes become your own PM textbook.

    Lesson 1: What a PM actually does

    A product manager is responsible for what gets built and why. Engineers decide how to build it, and designers decide how it looks and feels. The PM makes sure the team is solving a problem that matters, for the right users, in a way that also works for the business.

    The PM usually has no authority over anyone. They lead through clarity, evidence, and trust, which makes the job closer to “chief decision-explainer” than “boss.”

    The core loop

    The loop never ends: what you learn from one release shapes your understanding of users for the next.

    An example from trading

    Say Zerodha notices that many new F&O traders quit within 3 months.

    • A weak PM says, “Let’s build an options strategy builder!” That jumps straight to a solution.
    • A strong PM asks why they quit first. Is it losses? Confusing margin rules? The fear of a surprise square-off? Each cause leads to a completely different product. Losses might point to education or risk warnings. Margin confusion might point to a clearer margin preview before an order is placed.

    Falling in love with the problem, not the solution is the single most important PM habit.

    Why your trading background helps

    You already work with probabilistic thinking, risk and reward, acting on incomplete information, and a feedback loop where results show up in numbers. Those are PM skills. You also know broker platforms from a power user’s side, which is genuine domain insight for fintech roles.

    First exercise

    Pick one product you use as a trader, such as Kite, Sensibull, TradingView, or Quicko, and answer three questions:

    Grade your answers with the rubric in the PM Training Program doc, or paste them into the Weekly review prompt in any AI tool. Then compare them with the worked example below.

    Worked example: your Quicko answers, critiqued

    These were your first answers to the exercise, followed by the critique an interviewer would give. Verdict: strong enough for a first-round product sense question. Segmenting users and adding a “why it matters” line would make it stand out.

    Your answers

    1. Main user and job: people who want to file their own tax returns more easily than on the Income Tax portal. They hire Quicko to file their ITR without errors, in a way that’s easy to understand.
    2. Frustration: Quicko can’t complete every section of the ITR. Some sections have to be filled on the government portal, and Quicko doesn’t guide you through them.
    3. Underlying problem: Quicko promises to file your taxes in 15 minutes but doesn’t say what’s excluded and must be done by hand. You expected to do everything in Quicko.

    What worked

    • You found the real problem, not a feature request. Most people would say “Quicko should support every section.” You went deeper: the pain is a broken expectation. The “15 minutes” promise made you believe everything happens in one place. That’s an insight about trust, and interviewers notice it.
    • Your frustration was specific and lived. Real user insight sounds like this.

    What to sharpen

    Answer Gap Stronger version
    1 Users aren’t segmented A salaried employee filing ITR-1 and an F&O trader filing ITR-3 need very different things. Name the segment
    1 The emotional job is missing People hire Quicko to feel confident they won’t get a tax notice, without paying a CA
    2 Too vague Name the exact sections you had to fill on the portal. That turns a complaint into evidence
    3 Two problems are mixed together A coverage gap (unsupported sections, expensive to fix) and a communication gap (no upfront list or guidance, cheap to fix)

    Fixing the communication gap removes much of the pain even before any new section is built. Spotting the cheapest fix that removes the most pain is exactly the judgment PM interviews test.

    The answer, rewritten as a problem statement

    Use the template who + what they struggle with + when + why it matters:

    Users with complex returns, such as F&O traders filing ITR-3, find out midway through filing that parts of their return can’t be completed in Quicko, and get no guidance on what’s left or how to finish it. This breaks trust at the most anxious moment of the process and risks incomplete or incorrect filings.

    Follow-up questions to expect

    • “How would you know how many users hit this?” Track how many users leave Quicko for the portal mid-filing, count support tickets that mention manual sections, and compare completion rates for ITR-3 and ITR-1 filers.
    • “Which segment matters more to Quicko’s business?” Complex filers may be fewer, but they often pay more and complain louder. This is a prioritisation question (cheat sheet 4).

    Lesson 2: Segmentation, guesstimates and problem layers

    These three skills turn a vague product opinion into a sharp, defensible answer. Interviews test all three directly.

    1. Segmenting users

    The rule: segment by what changes the user’s need. Age and city rarely change what someone needs from a product. A 25-year-old and a 50-year-old with the same Form 16 need the same thing from Quicko.

    Use these axes, in rough order of value:

    1. Needs and complexity: what job they’re doing and how hard it is
    2. Behaviour: how they use the product today (first-timer or repeat, alone or with a CA)
    3. Value to the business: who pays, how much, and who stays year after year
    4. Demographics: only when they actually change the need

    Quicko, segmented by need:

    Segment ITR form What they need Main fear
    Salaried, one employer ITR-1 Speed, autofill from Form 16 Missing a deduction
    Salaried and investing ITR-2 Capital gains computed from broker statements Getting capital gains wrong
    F&O or active trader ITR-3 Business income, turnover, audit handling A tax notice, or an audit mistake
    Freelancer or consultant ITR-4 or ITR-3 Presumptive tax, advance tax Paying too much or too little

    Test of a good segmentation: each segment needs a different solution. If two segments need the same thing, merge them.

    Then choose a segment to focus on, scoring each one on four questions:

    • Size: how many of these users exist?
    • Pain: how badly does the product fail them today?
    • Value: will they pay more or stay longer?
    • Fit: can the company realistically serve them well?

    F&O traders are fewer than salaried users, but they feel more pain, pay more, and Quicko already has broker integrations. That makes a strong case for focusing on them.

    2. Guesstimates

    The interviewer doesn’t care about your final number. They’re watching how you structure the problem and whether your assumptions are reasonable.

    1. Clarify what’s being estimated: which country, which period, users or revenue.
    2. Pick a structure. Top-down starts from a large population and narrows with percentages. Bottom-up starts from one unit and multiplies (for example, filings per tax-help centre per day × number of centres).
    3. State every assumption out loud, with a one-line reason.
    4. Use round numbers. 1 crore is easier to work with than 1.13 crore, and precision adds nothing.
    5. Sanity-check the result, and cross-check it another way if you can.

    Worked example: how many Quicko users hit the manual-section problem each year? The numbers are illustrative assumptions, which is exactly how you’d present them in an interview.

    Step Assumption Result
    Individuals trading F&O in a year about 1 crore 1 crore
    Share who file an ITR reporting it 70% 70 lakh
    Share who self-file with a tool, not a CA 30% 21 lakh
    Quicko’s share of those tool users 15% about 3 lakh
    Share whose return needs a section Quicko doesn’t support 40% about 1.2 lakh users

    Sanity check: that’s about 1.2 lakh frustrated, high-value users a year. If Quicko gets far fewer support tickets than this suggests, either the 40% is too high or users are quietly leaving instead of complaining. Both are worth knowing.

    Common mistakes: going silent while you calculate, using overly precise numbers, and not explaining why you chose a percentage.

    3. Separating problems into layers

    Ask “why” five times until you reach something a team can change:

    • Symptom: the user ends up on the ITR portal, confused.
    • Why? They don’t know which sections are left.
    • Why? Quicko doesn’t show what it covers and what it doesn’t.
    • Why? The product and its “15 minutes” message were designed for simple filers.
    • Why? The company grew by serving salaried users first, so complex filers were never the main focus.

    Each “why” reveals a different layer:

    Layer The problem at this layer Kind of fix Cost
    Symptom User is confused on the portal Support articles Low
    Communication No upfront list of what’s excluded A coverage checklist and a step-by-step portal guide Low
    Product coverage Some sections are unsupported Build the missing sections High
    Strategy The product was built for another segment Decide whether complex filers are a priority Leadership decision

    Two tests that you’ve separated them properly:

    1. Independence test: if you fixed only this layer, would some of the pain go away? If yes, it’s a separate problem.
    2. Owner test: different layers usually belong to different people. Copy and guides sit with design and content, new sections with engineering, segment focus with leadership. Same owner and same fix means it’s one problem.

    Why it matters: layering shows you the cheapest fix that removes the most pain. Saying “I’d ship the coverage checklist this month while we decide whether to build full ITR-3 support” is exactly the judgment companies hire for.

    Practice: how many people use Zerodha Kite on a typical trading day?

    Try it yourself first, out loud, in 15 minutes. Then compare your structure with this one. The numbers are assumptions to replace with better data. NSE publishes each broker’s active-client count, which you can use to check the starting number.

    Step Assumption Result
    Zerodha active clients (traded in the last 12 months) about 70 lakh 70 lakh
    Active traders (intraday, F&O) 25% of clients, opening Kite on 80% of trading days 14 lakh a day
    Investors 75% of clients, opening Kite about once a week (20% of trading days) 10.5 lakh a day
    Daily users Sum of the two segments about 25 lakh

    Sanity check: about a third of active clients on a typical day is plausible for an app where many users trade every day. Notice how splitting users into two segments with different habits made the estimate far more believable than one blanket percentage.

    Lesson 3: Running user interviews that tell the truth

    Week 2 of the program. By the end you can find the right people, run a 30-minute interview without leading them, and take notes you can trust.

    Find the right people

    Interview people in the segment you’re testing, not whoever is easiest to reach. For Melange, a useful first segment is salaried people who have run at least one SIP for a year and choose their own funds. Write a two-question screener (“Do you invest through a monthly SIP? Who decides which funds?”) and only book people who pass it.

    Places to find them: people who signed up on melangeresearch.com, friends of friends (not close friends, who will be kind rather than honest), colleagues from past jobs, LinkedIn, and investing communities such as r/IndiaInvestments. Expect about one interview for every two or three requests, so send 8 requests to book 3. Offer something small in return, such as a summary of what you learn.

    Ask about the past, not the future

    People are poor at predicting what they’ll do, and polite when you show them your idea. So ask what they did, not what they would do.

    Weak Better
    “Would you use a monthly email that tells you where to invest?” “Tell me about the last time you changed or stopped a SIP.”
    “Is choosing between equity and gold hard?” “How did you decide how much to put into gold last year?”
    “Would you pay ₹199 a month?” “What do you pay today for advice or tools, and what for?”

    Then follow the energy. When an answer carries emotion (“I panicked”, “I hate that”), ask “What happened next?” or “Why was that hard?”, then stay quiet. Silence gets the best answers.

    Take notes you can trust

    Keep four kinds of notes apart: what they did, what they said word for word, what they think, and your own interpretation, marked as yours. Most bad research comes from mixing these up, then quoting your interpretation as if the user said it.

    Worked example

    You ask, “When did you last change your SIP?” She says, “In 2022. My portfolio was red for months, so I paused it.” You ask, “What did you do with the money?” “Left it in savings. I restarted about six months later, when things looked better.” That’s a fact (she paused for six months), a quote (“My portfolio was red”) and a hint of a job: reassure me when the market falls, so I don’t stop at the worst time. A question about your email feature would have told you none of this.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Pitching Melange in the first 20 minutes. Show it, if at all, only at the end.
    • Asking two questions at once, or answering for them (“…because it’s confusing, right?”).
    • Treating one strong opinion as a pattern. Wait for repeats.

    Exercise

    Write 5 assumptions about Melange’s users, a screener, and a 30-minute guide from the Templates tab. Rehearse once with the Simulation prompt, with the AI playing a SIP investor who gives vague answers.

    Check yourself

    1. Why is “Would you pay for this?” a weak question?
    2. What are the four kinds of notes?
    3. You need 3 interviews. How many requests should you send?

    Answers: 1. It asks about the future and invites politeness; ask what they pay today. 2. Facts, quotes, opinions and your interpretation. 3. About 8.

    Lesson 4: From notes to insights

    Week 3. By the end you can turn raw interview notes into a few strong insights, and choose which problem to solve.

    From observations to insights

    An observation is one thing one person said or did. An insight is a pattern across people that surprises you, backed by evidence, with a clear implication. “Users find investing stressful” is not an insight; everyone knows it. “4 of 5 people paused their SIP after a red month, and none had a rule for when to restart” is one: it’s specific, counted, and points somewhere.

    The synthesis steps

    1. Write every observation on its own line (one per sticky note, or one per spreadsheet row), with the participant number.
    2. Group similar lines without deciding the groups in advance (affinity mapping). Name each group in the user’s language.
    3. For each group, write the insight in one sentence, count how many participants it covers, and pick the best quote.
    4. Size each insight by frequency (how many), pain (how much it costs them) and reach (how many users like them exist).
    5. Look for evidence that disagrees with you, and say so in the report.

    Opportunity solution tree

    Put your goal at the top (for example, members keep investing every month and trust where it goes). Under it, place opportunities: the user needs and pains your insights revealed. Only then add 2–3 solutions per opportunity, and a cheap experiment for each. The tree stops you jumping from a goal straight to a feature you already liked.

    Worked example

    Five interviews give you about 60 observations, which group into four clusters:

    Cluster Participants Pain
    Pause SIPs after a bad month 4 of 5 High: they miss the recovery
    Unsure how much gold to hold 3 of 5 Medium
    Too many apps and tips 3 of 5 Low to medium
    Don’t trust advice without reasons 2 of 5 High for those two

    The first cluster wins on frequency and pain, so it becomes the target opportunity. Your headline: Investors don’t stop SIPs for lack of information; they stop because they feel alone after a fall.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Counting mentions instead of people: one talkative person can fill a cluster.
    • Writing insights as solutions (“Users need an app that…”).
    • Building personas from imagination rather than from your clusters.

    Exercise

    Cluster your five interviews, write the top 5 insights with evidence, draw Melange’s opportunity solution tree, and draft the insight report from the template.

    Check yourself

    1. What makes an observation an insight?
    2. Which three factors size an opportunity?
    3. Why add evidence that disagrees with you?

    Answers: 1. It’s a counted pattern across people that surprises you and has an implication. 2. Frequency, pain and reach. 3. It shows the reader you tested your own conclusion, which makes the rest believable.

    Lesson 5: Strategy, competition and positioning

    Week 4. By the end you can explain where Melange should play and how it wins, compare it honestly with competitors, and size its market.

    Strategy is choosing

    A strategy names a target customer, the problem you’ll solve for them, and why you’ll win, and it says what you won’t do. “Be the best investing app” isn’t a strategy, because it rules nothing out. “Win salaried SIP investors who want one clear monthly answer with the evidence shown, and stay out of stock tips and trading” is one.

    Three kinds of competitor

    • Direct: do the same job for the same people, such as paid fund-advisory services.
    • Indirect: do the job differently, such as investing apps with fund screeners and ratings (for example ET Money, Groww or Kuvera), or research sites such as Value Research and Morningstar India.
    • Substitutes: what people do instead, such as a relative’s advice, a mutual fund distributor, finfluencer videos, a spreadsheet, or doing nothing.

    Substitutes are usually the real competition for a new product. Doing nothing is free and feels safe.

    Positioning

    Positioning answers “Why you, for whom, compared with what?”. Start from what customers would use if you didn’t exist, list what’s genuinely different about you, turn each difference into value for the customer, and find the customers who care most. Then write: For [best-fit customers] who [need], [product] is a [category] that [key value]. Unlike [main alternative], we [unique attribute].

    Market sizing, worked for Melange

    AMFI reported 10.02 crore contributing SIP accounts in August 2026, with ₹32,297 crore invested through SIPs that month. One person often holds several SIP accounts, so convert accounts to people first:

    Step Assumption Result
    SIP accounts AMFI, August 2026 10 crore
    Accounts per investor about 3 3.3 crore investors (TAM)
    Decide their own split between shares and gold, and read research online in English 10% 33 lakh (SAM)
    Realistic share in 3 years 0.5% of SAM about 16,500 members (SOM)

    Every assumption is a guess to test. Saying so is part of a good answer.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Comparing feature lists instead of the jobs customers hire each product for.
    • Starting TAM from “all Indians” or “all investors”.
    • Copying a competitor’s flagship feature without evidence that your users need it.

    Exercise

    Write Melange’s one-line vision and three strategic bets. Tear down three competitors with the template. Write the positioning statement, then size the market with your own assumptions.

    Check yourself

    1. What must every strategy rule out?
    2. Name one substitute for Melange.
    3. Why convert SIP accounts to investors?

    Answers: 1. Customers, problems or approaches you won’t pursue. 2. A relative’s advice, a distributor, finfluencers, a spreadsheet or doing nothing. 3. One person often holds several accounts, so counting accounts overstates the market.

    Lesson 6: Prioritising and planning a roadmap

    Week 5. By the end you can rank a backlog with evidence, say no with reasons, and build a roadmap of outcomes.

    Every yes is a no to something else

    You have limited time, and as a solo founder the limit is your own hours. Prioritising means comparing each idea with the best other use of that time, not asking whether the idea is good.

    RICE, used honestly

    Score each idea on reach (members affected per quarter), impact (3 massive to 0.25 minimal), confidence (100%, 80% or 50%, based on evidence, not hope) and effort (person-weeks). RICE = reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort. Confidence is where people cheat: an idea with no user evidence deserves 50%, however much you like it.

    Use RICE to start the conversation, then check the top items against your insight report. If the highest score doesn’t touch your strongest insight, ask why.

    Other tools

    • Cost of delay for anything with a deadline: tax season, a regulatory date, or a market event.
    • MoSCoW to fix the scope of one release.
    • Kano to separate basics (users are angry without them) from delighters.

    Now, Next, Later

    Write each roadmap item as an outcome with a measure: “Members stay invested through a bad month (SIP pauses among members fall below 5%)”, not “Build a monthly email”. Now is committed, Next is validated and taking shape, Later is still being explored and has no dates.

    Worked example

    Idea Reach Impact Confidence Effort (weeks) RICE
    Email the monthly answer on release day 400 2 80% 2 320
    “What happened in past falls” note in each answer 400 2 50% 1 400
    Shares-versus-gold chart for your own years 300 1 80% 1 240
    Full portfolio tracker 200 2 50% 10 20

    The “past falls” note scores highest and also matches your strongest insight (people pause after a bad month), so it goes into Now. The portfolio tracker goes into Later, with the reason written down.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Giving every idea 100% confidence.
    • A roadmap of features with dates and no outcomes.
    • Saying “not now” without saying what would change your mind.

    Exercise

    Put every Melange idea, bug and request into one backlog, score it with RICE, check the top 5 against your insights, write “not doing, and why” for the bottom 5, and draft the Now/Next/Later roadmap.

    Check yourself

    1. What does confidence measure in RICE?
    2. How do you write a roadmap item?
    3. When is cost of delay the right tool?

    Answers: 1. How much evidence supports your reach and impact estimates. 2. As an outcome with a measure, not a feature. 3. When the value of the work drops sharply after a date.

    Lesson 7: Metrics that matter

    Week 6. By the end you can choose Melange’s north-star metric, its inputs and guardrails, and read a funnel and a retention curve.

    Choosing a north star

    A good north star measures value delivered to users, moves within weeks, can be influenced by the team, and is hard to fake. For a product people use once a month, a daily metric makes no sense. “Members who read that month’s answer within 7 days of release” fits Melange: it shows the core value was delivered, on a monthly rhythm.

    Then add inputs the team can move (new members who set their monthly amount and years, answer emails opened, chart pages read per visit), guardrails that must not get worse (page load time, data errors, complaints) and a counter-metric that catches harm (SIPs stopped or switched after a bad month).

    Reading a funnel

    Write each step, count the people who reach it, and find the biggest drop. Illustrative numbers for one month:

    Step People Carried on from the step before
    Visited melangeresearch.com 2,000
    Created an account 200 10%
    Set monthly amount and years 120 60%
    Read their first answer 90 75%
    Read the next month’s answer 60 67%

    The weakest step is visit to sign-up at 10%, so that’s where to look first, but only after checking whether the visitors were the right people at all.

    Retention

    Group members by the month they joined (a cohort) and plot the share who read each later month’s answer. A healthy curve drops early, then flattens. If it never flattens, the product isn’t yet delivering repeat value, and no amount of acquisition will fix that.

    Instrumenting

    Name events as object_action in the past tense (account_created, monthly_amount_set, answer_viewed) with the properties you’ll need later. Decide the questions first, then the events.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Picking page views or sign-ups as the north star.
    • Tracking 40 events and reading none of them.
    • Celebrating a rise in the north star while the counter-metric rises too.

    Exercise

    Propose Melange’s north star and 3 inputs, map the funnel from first visit to habitual use, define “retained”, add 2 guardrails, write the tracking plan, and install a free analytics tool.

    Check yourself

    1. Why is a daily metric wrong for Melange?
    2. What does a flattening retention curve tell you?
    3. What’s a counter-metric for?

    Answers: 1. Members need it once a month, so daily use would measure the wrong behaviour. 2. A core group keeps finding value. 3. Catching harm or gaming caused by pushing the main metric.

    Lesson 8: Data and experiments with little traffic

    Week 7. By the end you can answer product questions with SQL, write an experiment brief, and pick a test method that suits Melange’s traffic.

    Questions first, then SQL

    Start from the decision you need to make, write the question in plain words, and only then write the query. Five questions worth answering for Melange: How many members read each month’s answer? How long after release do they read it? Which sign-up month keeps members best? Do members who set their amount and years come back more? Which pages do visitors see before signing up? The SQL patterns in cheat sheet 6 cover all five with SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY and one JOIN.

    What an A/B test needs

    Split users at random, choose one primary metric and your guardrails before you start, fix the sample size in advance, and don’t stop early because the result looks good.

    A rule of thumb for sample size per group is 16 × p × (1 − p) ÷ d², where p is today’s conversion rate and d is the smallest change worth detecting. With 10% sign-up conversion and a 2-point change (10% to 12%), that’s 16 × 0.1 × 0.9 ÷ 0.0004 = 3,600 visitors in each group. If Melange gets 2,000 visitors a month, a clean A/B test on sign-ups would take almost four months.

    When traffic is low

    • Before and after with a holdout: ship to most members, keep a small group without the change, and compare.
    • Fake door: add a button for a feature that doesn’t exist yet, and count clicks.
    • Do it by hand first: send the “past falls” note manually to 10 members and interview them.
    • Five-user usability tests: watch people use the page and count where they get stuck.

    Diagnosing a metric drop

    Check that the drop is real (tracking, definitions, a broken data feed), find when it started, look for internal causes (a release, a bug, a change in the email) and external ones (a market fall, a holiday, a competitor), segment it (new or existing members, device, source), find the funnel step, and confirm one hypothesis with data before fixing it.

    Worked example

    Hypothesis: if members get the monthly answer by email on release day, the share who read it within 7 days will rise from 60% to 75%, because they won’t have to remember to visit. Method: with 120 members, a holdout is better than an A/B test: send the email to 100, hold back 20, compare after two monthly cycles. Guardrails: unsubscribe rate, complaints. Decision rule: keep it if the emailed group reads at least 10 points more without more complaints.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Running an A/B test on a few hundred users and trusting the result.
    • Changing two things at once, so you can’t tell which one worked.
    • Deciding the success metric after seeing the data.

    Exercise

    Load one Melange dataset into DB Browser for SQLite, answer the five questions above, write an experiment brief for one roadmap item, and choose the right test method for your traffic.

    Check yourself

    1. Why fix the sample size before starting?
    2. What’s a holdout group?
    3. What should you check first when a metric drops?

    Answers: 1. So you don’t stop early on a lucky result. 2. A small group that doesn’t get the change, kept for comparison. 3. Whether the drop is real: tracking, definitions and data feeds.

    Lesson 9: Writing specs people can build from

    Week 8. By the end you can write a PRD with clear acceptance criteria, list edge cases, and sketch the main flow.

    What a PRD is for

    A PRD (product requirements document) makes the problem, the goal and the definition of done impossible to misread. It isn’t a design or a technical plan; it leaves the “how” to the people building it. As a solo builder you are both PM and engineer, and writing the PRD still pays: it forces you to decide what “done” means before you start coding.

    The parts that matter most

    • Problem and evidence: one paragraph, with numbers and quotes from your research.
    • Goal and success metric: the number you’ll check after launch, and by when.
    • Non-goals: what this deliberately won’t do, so scope doesn’t creep.
    • User stories with acceptance criteria: “As a member, I want [capability], so that [benefit]”, each with a Given / When / Then test.
    • Edge cases and error states: what happens when things go wrong.
    • Regulatory impact: for Melange, anything that could read as personal advice.

    Worked example: the monthly answer email

    Story: as a member, I want this month’s answer in my inbox on release day, so that I don’t have to remember to check.

    Acceptance criteria:

    • Given a member has set their monthly amount and years, when the month’s research is published, then they get one email with that month’s answer, the main reason in one sentence, and a link to the full evidence.
    • Given a member has unsubscribed, when research is published, then no email is sent.
    • Given the research is delayed, when the usual release day passes, then no email goes out until the research is final.

    Edge cases: a data source is late or wrong; a member changed their amount mid-month; a brand-new member joins the day before release; the email provider fails; the wording could read as personalised advice.

    Wireframes

    Sketch the flow in boxes before any visual design: where the member starts, each screen, and each decision. Excalidraw or Figma’s free plan is enough. Review the flow with a user before polishing anything.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Starting with the solution and writing the problem afterwards to justify it.
    • Acceptance criteria that can’t be tested (“it should be fast”).
    • Forgetting non-goals, then building them anyway.

    Exercise

    Write the PRD for your top Now item from Week 5, with user stories, acceptance criteria and edge cases. Wireframe the main flow, then run a tech review with the Simulation prompt, with the AI as a senior engineer.

    Check yourself

    1. What does a PRD leave out on purpose?
    2. Rewrite “the page should load fast” as a testable criterion.
    3. Why list non-goals?

    Answers: 1. How it’s built. 2. For example: “the answer page loads in under 2 seconds on a 4G phone”. 3. To stop scope creeping into the release.

    Lesson 10: Shipping and launching safely

    Week 9. By the end you can cut a feature to its smallest useful version, ship it, launch it safely and learn from it.

    Ship the smallest useful version

    Ask “What’s the smallest version that tests whether this works?” For the monthly email, that might be a plain-text email sent by hand from a list, before any automation. If members read it and act on it, build it properly.

    Building with AI coding tools

    AI coding tools let a PM build real features, but you own the result. Write the acceptance criteria first, review every change, test the edge cases yourself, and keep changes small enough to undo.

    The launch plan

    • Goal and metric agreed and written down, with the dashboard live before launch.
    • Rollout: yourself first, then 10 members, then everyone.
    • Kill switch: a way to turn it off without a new release.
    • Rollback: what you’ll do if it goes wrong.
    • Communication: release notes that lead with the benefit, and an answer ready for the likely questions.
    • Compliance check for any new claim or wording.
    • Review dates one week and four weeks after launch.

    Agree go / no-go criteria in advance and launch only if every one is met.

    After launch

    Compare the metric with the goal at one week and four weeks. Then run a retro: what went well, what didn’t, what you’ll change, each action with an owner and a date. If something broke, write a blameless post-mortem: timeline, impact, root cause from the 5 Whys, and fixes to the system rather than blame.

    Worked example: release notes

    New: this month’s answer now arrives in your inbox on release day, with the main reason in one line. You don’t need to do anything; reply “stop” to turn it off. One benefit, one line, and what the member needs to do.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Launching to everyone at once with no way back.
    • No metric agreed before launch, so success gets defined afterwards.
    • Release notes that describe the feature instead of the benefit.

    Exercise

    Break the PRD into a backlog, build the smallest useful version, write the launch plan, ship, write release notes and a weekly update, then hold the retro and set up the dashboard.

    Check yourself

    1. Why decide go / no-go criteria before launch day?
    2. What’s a kill switch for?
    3. What should release notes lead with?

    Answers: 1. So the decision isn’t swayed by launch-day excitement. 2. Turning a feature off instantly without a new release. 3. The benefit to the user.

    Lesson 11: How software and AI models work

    Week 10. By the end you can draw Melange’s system map, reason about cost and failure, and explain how large language models work.

    The pieces of a product like Melange

    • Client: the website in the member’s browser.
    • Server and database: run the logic and store accounts, members’ settings and research results.
    • Data pipelines: fetch market and economic data from official sources on a schedule.
    • Research models: turn that data into the monthly answer.
    • Accounts and sign-in: email and password, or Google sign-in (OAuth), which shares only name, email and profile picture.
    • Hosting, DNS and CDN: serve the site quickly and safely. Melange’s domain, for example, runs through Cloudflare.

    Draw your real stack, then mark where it can fail (a data source changes format, the sign-in provider is down, a scheduled job doesn’t run) and what each part costs per month.

    How large language models work

    • A model reads and writes tokens, chunks of text of roughly 4 characters in English. Price and limits are counted in tokens.
    • The context window is how much text it can consider at once: your instructions, the data you give it and the conversation.
    • It predicts likely text, so it can be fluent and wrong at the same time (a hallucination).
    • Temperature sets randomness: low for consistent answers, higher for creative ones.
    • It has no memory between calls unless you send the history.

    Prompting, RAG or fine-tuning

    Start with prompting. Use RAG (retrieving your own documents into the prompt) when answers must use your data, such as this month’s research, and cite it. Use fine-tuning only for a consistent style or format on a narrow task at scale, when prompting isn’t enough. Agents that call tools over many steps are powerful but hard to test; keep a human approval step for anything risky.

    Worked example: cost

    An explainer that sends a 1,500-token prompt and gets a 300-token answer uses 1,800 tokens per question. If 1,000 members each ask 3 questions a month, that’s 5.4 million tokens a month. Multiply by your model’s price per million tokens (input and output are often priced differently) to get the monthly cost, then divide by members to get cost per member.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Treating AI output as fact without a source.
    • Picking the biggest model by default, when a smaller one passes your evals.
    • Forgetting that every AI call adds cost and waiting time.

    Exercise

    Draw Melange’s system map, list its failure points and running costs, list where Melange uses AI today or could, assess one AI feature on accuracy, cost and speed, and write the AI opportunity memo.

    Check yourself

    1. When is RAG the right choice?
    2. Why can a confident AI answer be wrong?
    3. What two numbers give you AI cost per member?

    Answers: 1. When answers must use your own or fresh data and cite it. 2. It predicts likely text rather than checking facts. 3. Tokens used per member per month and the price per token.

    Lesson 12: Building an AI feature people can trust

    Week 11. By the end you can spec an AI feature, build an evaluation set, and design for the times it’s wrong.

    Start from the user problem

    Members don’t need “AI”. They need to understand why this month’s answer says what it says. An explainer that answers questions about the monthly research, using only that research, is a good candidate: the facts already exist, and AI only has to explain them in plain words.

    Decide what it must never do

    For Melange, the explainer must never give personalised advice (“you should move your SIP to…”), invent numbers, or answer from outside the month’s research. Write these rules first. They shape the prompt, the evals and the interface.

    Evals: how you know it works

    1. Collect 30 real questions members might ask, such as “Why is this month mostly gold?”.
    2. For each, write the key facts a good answer must contain and the pass criteria.
    3. Score every output 0 (fail), 1 (partly right) or 2 (pass), and track accuracy, grounding in the research, and advice violations separately.
    4. Set launch thresholds in advance, for example at least 90% passes and zero advice violations.
    5. Rerun the evals on every prompt or model change.

    You can use another model to grade outputs (LLM-as-judge), but check its grades against your own on a sample first.

    Design for being wrong

    Show the source for each claim, say “I don’t know” when the research doesn’t cover the question, keep the tone plain rather than certain, and give members an easy way to flag a bad answer.

    Worked example: one eval row

    Question Key facts Pass criteria Score
    “Why is this month mostly gold?” The two main reasons given in the research Accurate, uses only the research, no personal advice 0–2

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Testing on five friendly questions and calling it done.
    • Letting the model produce numbers instead of quoting them from your data.
    • Launching without thresholds, so any result looks good enough.

    Exercise

    Write 30 test cases for one Melange AI feature, run the eval and score it, design how the feature shows sources and confidence, estimate cost per member, and write the AI feature spec.

    Check yourself

    1. Why write the “never do” rules first?
    2. What three things do you score separately?
    3. When do you rerun evals?

    Answers: 1. They shape the prompt, the evals and the interface. 2. Accuracy, grounding and advice violations. 3. On every prompt or model change.

    Lesson 13: Compliance as product work

    Week 12. By the end you can spot the rules that shape a fintech product, run a compliance review of Melange, and design with compliance from the start. This is a study guide, not legal advice.

    Why compliance is a product question

    In fintech the rules decide what you can say, to whom, and what data you may keep. A PM who brings compliance in at the end ships late or not at all. A PM who designs with it ships safely and earns trust.

    Melange’s central question

    SEBI regulates investment advice and research. Melange says it offers general research and isn’t registered as an investment adviser or research analyst. The question to settle is whether an answer “ranked for your monthly amount and your years” counts as personalised advice. A disclaimer doesn’t change what the product actually does, so the review must look at the substance.

    Ways to resolve it include: keeping the research general (the same answer for everyone in a broad group), registering, or partnering with a registered adviser for any personalised part. Each changes the product, its cost and its pricing. The decision needs a qualified lawyer; your job is to frame it clearly.

    Data and marketing

    • DPDP Act and Rules: collect only what you need, explain why, get consent, keep data secure and let people delete it. Most obligations apply from May 13, 2027, so building this in now is cheap.
    • Marketing claims: avoid “guaranteed”, “safe” or past returns presented as a promise.
    • Germany and the EU: personalised investment recommendations generally fall under MiFID II and BaFin licensing, and personal data under GDPR.

    Worked example: a compliance review entry

    Rule: SEBI investment adviser rules. Applies? Unsure. Why: the monthly answer is ranked by each member’s amount and years. Options: make the answer general for broad groups; register; partner. Question for a lawyer: does ranking by amount and horizon make it personalised advice? Change now: remove any wording that sounds like an instruction to a specific person.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Treating a disclaimer as protection.
    • Asking compliance questions the week before launch.
    • Storing data “in case it’s useful later”.

    Exercise

    Map where Melange sits in India’s financial system, list the SEBI rules that may apply, audit the personal data Melange stores, list what would change for German users, and write the compliance review from the template.

    Check yourself

    1. Why doesn’t a disclaimer settle the advice question?
    2. Name three DPDP habits to build in now.
    3. Who should make the final call on registration?

    Answers: 1. Regulators look at what the product does, not what the label says. 2. Collect only what’s needed, get consent, allow deletion (also: explain purpose, keep it secure). 3. A qualified lawyer, with you framing the options.

    Lesson 14: Leading without authority

    Week 13. By the end you can map stakeholders, write a decision memo, run a decision meeting and present a quarterly business review.

    Stakeholders

    List everyone who affects or is affected by Melange: members, people who may join, data providers, a compliance adviser, anyone who builds with you, and future partners. Place each on a power × interest grid and decide how you’ll keep each one involved. Talk to the key people before the meeting where a decision is made, so the meeting confirms rather than surprises.

    Writing that drives decisions

    Lead with the answer (the pyramid principle): recommendation first, then three reasons, then detail. A decision memo states the context, two or three real options with their trade-offs, your recommendation, and who decides by when.

    Disagreement

    Argue with data, separate the person from the problem, find the goal you share, then debate the path. Once the decision is made, commit to it, even if you argued for something else. Escalate early, bringing options rather than complaints.

    Worked example: a decision memo

    Decision: should Melange charge for the research preview this quarter? Recommendation: not yet; first prove that members read and act on the answer for three months. Options: (A) charge now, which tests willingness to pay but adds compliance risk before the advice question is settled; (B) stay free for one more quarter and measure retention; (C) offer a paid tier only for the general research. Trade-off: B delays revenue by a quarter. Decided by: you, by the end of the month, after one call with a lawyer.

    The quarterly business review
