    One page: the headline, goals against results, the north star and its inputs, what shipped and what it changed, what didn’t work, the customer insight of the quarter, next quarter’s goals, and the risks or decisions you need.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Bringing a decision to a meeting nobody has seen before.
    • Memos that build up to the recommendation instead of starting with it.
    • Re-arguing a decision after it’s made.

    Exercise

    Map Melange’s stakeholders, write one decision memo, run the three-part quarter simulation with the Simulation prompt, and write the QBR memo from the template.

    Check yourself

    1. What goes first in a decision memo?
    2. Why talk to stakeholders before the meeting?
    3. What does “disagree and commit” mean?

    Answers: 1. The recommendation. 2. So the meeting confirms a decision instead of surprising people. 3. You argue your case, then fully support the decision once it’s made.

    Lesson 15: Turning your work into offers

    Week 14, and alongside the interview sprint. By the end you can show your work as proof, run a focused job search, and fix the part of your funnel that’s failing.

    How PM hiring works

    Most loops have a recruiter screen, a hiring-manager conversation, and then several rounds: product sense, metrics and execution, estimation or strategy, behavioural, and for AI roles an AI product round. Many companies add a take-home. Each round is scored on structure, judgment, user focus, use of data and communication, which is why answer structures matter so much.

    Your story

    Your arc is unusual and strong: a trader who decides under risk every day, who built two products (a personal trading platform and Melange Research), and who now wants to build for many more users in a team. Every answer should show product judgment, not just trading knowledge.

    Proof beats claims

    Turn your five best graded deliverables into one-page case studies: context, problem with evidence, what you did and why, result or learning, and what you’d do next. Put them on one public portfolio page and link it from your resume and LinkedIn. A hiring manager who reads one good case study already has evidence you can do the job.

    Run the search like a funnel

    Stage Healthy sign If it’s failing, fix…
    Applications → replies At least 1 reply in 10 tailored applications Targeting, resume headline, referrals
    Recruiter screen → next round Most screens pass Your 90-second story, salary and notice answers
    Interview rounds → offer You pass most rounds The weakest round type in your scorecard

    Referrals usually get more replies than cold applications, so ask for one whenever you know someone at the company. Follow up once after 5–7 days.

    Offers

    Research the range before any salary conversation, give a range whose bottom is your real target, and negotiate on the whole package: base pay, bonus, joining date, relocation and visa support for roles abroad, and learning budget.

    Mistakes to avoid

    • Sending 100 untailored applications instead of 30 tailored ones with referrals.
    • Telling the trading story without the product lessons.
    • Not reading the funnel, and so repeating the same failure.

    Exercise

    Run the five mock interviews this week, turn your five best deliverables into case studies, update your resume and LinkedIn, publish the portfolio page, and plan the next four weeks of your search.

    Check yourself

    1. What should you fix if 20 applications get no replies?
    2. What goes on a one-page case study?
    3. What can you negotiate besides base pay?

    Answers: 1. Targeting, resume and referrals. 2. Context, problem and evidence, what you did, result or learning, and next steps. 3. Bonus, joining date, relocation, learning budget.

    Cheat sheets

    One page of reference per topic: sheets 1 to 13 in the order the program covers them, then Melange’s market (14), the job search itself (15), trading and markets roles where your experience is the edge (16) and open-door roles where your skills transfer (17). Use them for each day’s Learn block, for revision before interviews, and on days when no AI tool is available.

    1. The PM role

    A PM decides what gets built and why, and makes sure it works for users and for the business. The PM has no authority over the team, so they lead with evidence, clear writing and trust.

    What a PM owns:

    • The problem: which user problem is worth solving now.
    • The outcome: what success means, in numbers.
    • The decisions: priorities and trade-offs, written down where everyone can see them.
    • Alignment: engineering, design, business and compliance all know the plan and the reasons for it.
    Role Owns Typical question
    Product manager What to build and why “Which problem should we solve next?”
    Engineer How it’s built “What’s the simplest reliable way to build this?”
    Designer How it works and feels for users “Where will users get confused?”
    Project or program manager When, and in what order “What’s blocking the launch date?”
    Product owner (in Scrum) One team’s backlog “Is this story ready for the sprint?”

    The core artifacts:

    Artifact Question it answers When
    Problem statement Who struggles with what, and why does it matter? Start of discovery
    Product brief (one-pager) Should we invest in this? Before committing a team
    Roadmap What are we doing now, next and later? Updated monthly or quarterly
    PRD What exactly are we building, and how will we know it worked? Before building
    Metrics dashboard Is it working? Checked weekly
    Launch plan and release notes How does it reach users safely? At launch
    Retro or post-mortem What did we learn? After a launch or an incident

    How the job grows with seniority:

    Level Scope
    Junior or Associate PM Delivers a well-defined feature well
    Mid-level PM Owns a problem area and its metrics from end to end
    Senior PM Sets strategy for an area, aligns leaders, and makes bigger bets

    Habits of strong PMs: love the problem, not your solution · write decisions down · act on imperfect data, then measure · say no more often than yes · judge yourself by outcomes, not by features shipped.

    2. Discovery and user research

    Discovery finds out which problems are real and worth solving before anything gets built. Its output is evidence, not features.

    Jobs-to-be-done (JTBD): people “hire” a product to make progress in a situation. Write each job as:

    When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].

    Example: When the market falls sharply just before my SIP date, I want to know whether to keep investing as planned, so I can stay on track without panicking. Every job has a functional side (get it done), an emotional side (feel safe, in control) and a social side (look competent).

    The Mom Test rules (Rob Fitzpatrick), for interviews that don’t mislead you:

    1. Talk about their life, not your idea.
    2. Ask about specific things they did in the past, not opinions about the future.
    3. Talk less and listen more.
    Weak question Better question
    “Would you use a site that tells you where each month’s SIP should go?” “Tell me about the last time you stopped or changed a SIP. What happened just before it?”
    “How much would you pay for this?” “What do you pay today for advice, apps or courses about your investments?”
    “Is choosing between shares and gold confusing?” “Walk me through how you chose the fund for your last SIP.”
    “Is this feature useful?” “What did you do the last time this problem came up?”

    A 30-minute interview: consent and intro (2 min) → their context and investing routine (5) → the last time the problem happened, in detail (15) → current workarounds and spending (5) → wrap-up: “Who else should I talk to?” (3).

    Taking notes: keep four kinds of notes apart: facts (what they did), quotes (their exact words), opinions (what they think), and your interpretation (marked as yours).

    Synthesis, in four steps:

    1. Write each observation on its own line or sticky note.
    2. Group similar observations (affinity mapping).
    3. Turn each group into an insight: a surprising truth about users, with evidence (“4 of 5 investors said…”).
    4. Size each insight by frequency, pain and reach.

    Opportunity solution tree (Teresa Torres): start from one outcome, branch into opportunities (user needs and pains), then solutions, then cheap experiments. Never jump straight from an outcome to a solution.

    Each solution traces back to a user need and forward to a cheap test, so nothing is built just because it sounds good.

    Usability testing (think-aloud): give users a task, not instructions; ask them to think out loud; don’t help; note every hesitation. Around five users usually reveal the biggest problems.

    3. Strategy and positioning

    Strategy is a set of choices about where to play and how to win. The roadmap is how you carry those choices out. The Melange examples below are illustrations to replace with your own.

    Term Question it answers Melange example (illustrative)
    Vision (5+ years) What world are we building toward? Every SIP investor in India knows, in plain words, where this month’s money should go and why
    Strategy (1–3 years) Where do we play, and how do we win? Win salaried SIP investors who want one clear monthly answer, using free economy and market charts to earn trust and showing the evidence behind every answer
    Goals or OKRs (a quarter) What must we achieve now? Objective: prove members trust the monthly answer. Key results: 200 research-preview members; 60% read the answer within 3 days of release; fewer than 5% stop their SIP after a bad month
    Roadmap What will we build, in what order? Now, Next and Later (cheat sheet 4)

    Competitive analysis: list three kinds of competitors. Direct competitors do the same job for the same users. Indirect competitors do the same job differently. Substitutes include spreadsheets, advice from family or a fund distributor, finfluencer videos, or doing nothing. For each one, note the target users, core job, key features, pricing, strengths, weaknesses, and what users say in app reviews.

    Product teardown checklist:

    • Onboarding: steps and time until the user first gets value
    • The core loop: what brings users back each day
    • Monetisation: where and when users are asked to pay
    • Retention hooks: alerts, streaks, reports
    • Trust signals: regulation, security, social proof
    • What you would change, and why

    Positioning (April Dunford’s five parts): competitive alternatives → your unique attributes → the value those attributes create → the best-fit customers → the market category. Then write it as one sentence:

    For [best-fit customers] who [need], [product] is a [category] that [key value]. Unlike [main alternative], we [unique attribute].

    How Indian fintechs make money:

    Model How money is made Typical example
    Brokerage Fee per order or share of turnover Discount brokers
    Subscription Monthly or yearly fee Analytics and strategy tools
    Interest Interest on balances or lending margin Lenders, neobanks
    Distribution commission Commission on mutual funds or insurance sold Investment apps
    Payments Merchant fees on cards (UPI is largely free for merchants) Payment gateways
    B2B and APIs Per call or licence fee Data and infrastructure providers

    Market sizing:

    • TAM (total addressable market): everyone who could have the need.
    • SAM (serviceable addressable market): the part your product and channels can reach.
    • SOM (serviceable obtainable market): what you can realistically win in 2–3 years.

    For Melange, TAM could start from the number of people in India who invest through SIPs (AMFI publishes SIP account numbers every month, and one person can hold several accounts). SAM narrows that to investors who decide their own split between shares and gold and read research online in English. SOM is a realistic share of SAM. State every assumption, as in a guesstimate.

    4. Prioritisation and roadmaps

    Prioritisation means choosing what not to do. Every yes takes time away from something else, so compare every idea with the best other use of the same team.

    RICE scoring:

    RICE score = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort

    • Reach: users affected per quarter.
    • Impact: 3 = massive, 2 = high, 1 = medium, 0.5 = low, 0.25 = minimal.
    • Confidence: 100% = high, 80% = medium, 50% = low.
    • Effort: person-weeks of work.

    Worked example for Melange (illustrative numbers):

    Idea Reach per quarter Impact Confidence Effort (person-weeks) RICE score
    Email the monthly answer on release day 400 2 80% 2 320
    Shares-versus-gold chart for your own years 300 1 80% 1 240
    AI explainer that answers questions about the monthly answer 600 1 50% 4 75
    Full portfolio tracker linked to fund statements 200 2 50% 10 20

    The cheap, confident ideas beat the impressive, expensive one. Treat RICE as a starting point for discussion, not a verdict, and check the top items against your user insights.

    Other frameworks:

    Framework Use it when Watch out for
    ICE (Impact × Confidence × Ease) Quickly scoring many small ideas, such as growth experiments Very subjective
    Kano model Sorting basics, performance features and delighters Needs survey data from users
    MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won’t) Fixing the scope of one release Everything drifts into “Must”
    Cost of delay Time-sensitive work: regulation deadlines, tax season, expiry-day changes Needs honest estimates
    Opportunity cost Any big bet Always name the alternative you’re giving up

    Now / Next / Later roadmaps:

    • Now: committed and being built.
    • Next: validated problems with solutions taking shape.
    • Later: opportunities still to explore, with no dates.

    Write roadmap items as outcomes, not features: “Help members stay invested through bad months”, not “Build a monthly email”.

    Saying no, politely and clearly:

    • “That’s a real problem. Right now we’re focused on [goal], and this would delay [item]. Can we look at it in the next roadmap review?”
    • “What problem would this solve? Let’s see where it ranks against what we’re doing now.”
    • “Not now, and here’s why. Here’s what would change my mind.”

    5. Metrics

    Good metrics show whether users get value and whether the business is healthy. Vanity metrics only make you feel good.

    Type What it is Melange example (illustrative)
    North-star metric The one number that best captures value delivered to users Members who read that month’s answer within 7 days of release
    Input metrics 3–5 levers that move the north star New members who set their monthly amount and years, answer emails opened, chart pages read per visit
    Guardrail metrics Must not get worse while you push the north star Page load time, data errors found after release, complaints
    Counter-metric Catches anyone gaming the main metric SIPs stopped or switched after a bad month (shouldn’t rise)
    Vanity metric Looks good but drives no decision Total page views, social media followers

    The team works on the inputs; the north star shows whether that work creates value; the guardrails make sure it doesn’t do harm.

    The AARRR funnel, with the question to ask at each stage:

    1. Acquisition: where do new visitors come from?
    2. Activation: do they create an account, set their monthly amount and years, and read their first answer?
    3. Retention: do they come back for next month’s answer?
    4. Referral: do they recommend Melange to friends who run SIPs?
    5. Revenue: do they pay, and does that cover the cost of serving them?

    Retention: a cohort is a group of users who started in the same week. Plot the share of each cohort still active over time. A healthy curve drops at first, then flattens. For a monthly product like Melange, measure retention month by month, not day by day.

    Key formulas:

    Metric Formula
    Conversion rate Users who complete a step ÷ users who reach it
    Week-N retention Cohort users active in week N ÷ cohort size
    Churn Users lost in a period ÷ users at the start
    Stickiness (DAU/MAU) Daily active users ÷ monthly active users
    ARPU Revenue ÷ users
    CAC Sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers
    LTV Monthly ARPU × gross margin × average lifetime in months
    LTV:CAC LTV ÷ CAC (3:1 is a common rule of thumb for health)

    A good metric is tied to user value, moves within weeks, can be acted on, is hard to game, and has an owner.

    6. Data, SQL and experiments

    You don’t need to be an analyst, but you must be able to pull basic numbers yourself and know when an experiment’s result can be trusted.

    SQL patterns (SQLite syntax, which works in free tools such as DB Browser for SQLite):

    -- Answers read per member in the last 90 days
SELECT member_id, COUNT(*) AS answers_read
FROM answer_views
WHERE viewed_on >= DATE('now', '-90 days')
GROUP BY member_id
ORDER BY answers_read DESC;

-- Monthly active members (read at least one answer that month)
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', viewed_on) AS month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT member_id) AS active_members
FROM answer_views
GROUP BY month;

-- Answers read per member, by segment (joining two tables)
SELECT m.segment,
       COUNT(v.member_id) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT m.member_id) AS answers_per_member
FROM members m
LEFT JOIN answer_views v ON v.member_id = m.member_id
GROUP BY m.segment
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT m.member_id) >= 30;

    Clauses always come in this order: SELECT → FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping.

    A/B test basics:

    • Write the hypothesis first: “If we [change], then [metric] will [rise or fall] by [amount], because [reason].”
    • Split users at random, not sessions.
    • Choose one primary metric and your guardrails before starting.
    • Decide the sample size and duration in advance with a free sample-size calculator. Run whole weeks, because behaviour differs by day; for a monthly product like Melange, run at least one full monthly cycle.
    • A p-value below 0.05 means a difference this large would be unlikely if the change had no real effect. It does not mean “95% chance the change works”.

    Common pitfalls: stopping early when the result looks good · tracking so many metrics that one “wins” by chance · novelty effects that fade · groups of unexpectedly different sizes (a sign something is broken) · unusual weeks such as budget day, results season or expiry changes.

    When traffic is too low for an A/B test (likely for Melange): compare before and after while holding back a small group · run a fake-door test (a button for a feature that doesn’t exist yet, to measure interest) · deliver the feature by hand to a few users first · run 5-user usability tests · roll out to a few users at a time · interview users about the change.

    When a metric drops, work through this checklist:

    1. Is it real? Check for tracking changes, data pipeline breaks, definition changes and dashboard bugs.
    2. When did it start? Was it sudden or gradual?
    3. Internal causes: a release, bug, pricing change, experiment or outage.
    4. External causes: a market holiday, low volatility, a competitor’s launch, a regulation change, or seasonality.
    5. Segment it: by platform, app version, region, new vs existing users, and user type.
    6. Find the funnel step where it breaks.
    7. Form a hypothesis, confirm it with data, fix it, and add an alert so you catch it sooner next time.

    7. Specs and design

    A good spec makes the problem and the definition of success impossible to misread, and leaves the “how” to engineers and designers.

    PRD outline (the full template is in the Templates tab):

    1. Problem and evidence
    2. Goals and success metrics
    3. Non-goals: what this deliberately won’t do
    4. Users and use cases
    5. Requirements, written as user stories with priorities
    6. User flow and designs
    7. Edge cases and error states
    8. Non-functional requirements: speed, reliability, security, compliance
    9. Analytics events to track
    10. Rollout plan
    11. Risks and open questions

    User stories: “As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit].” Good stories are INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable.

    Acceptance criteria (Given / When / Then):

    Given a member has set their monthly amount and years, when that month’s research is published, then Melange shows that month’s answer (shares, gold or a mix) in plain words, with the evidence behind it and a note that it is general research, not advice.

    Edge cases to check in any trading product:

    • Market closed, pre-open session, or a trading holiday
    • Broker or exchange API down, or very slow
    • Stale or missing price data
    • Orders partly filled or rejected
    • Expiry days, price-band limits and freeze quantities
    • Network lost mid-order, or a double tap creating duplicate orders
    • Broker session expired (many Indian broker APIs need a fresh login every day)
    • Corporate actions such as splits and bonuses
    • Very large or very small quantities

    Working with designers: share the problem and constraints, not your sketch of the solution · review the flow before the visuals · test with users early · agree on what “done” looks like.

    Working with engineers: bring them into discovery early · ask for options with trade-offs (“What’s the 20% version that gets 80% of the value?”) · treat estimates as ranges, not promises · protect time for fixing tech debt (many teams reserve 10–20%) · never change scope mid-sprint without agreeing what gets dropped.

    8. Delivery and launch

    Shipping is where plans meet reality. Your job is to keep the team unblocked, launch safely, and learn from what happens.

    Scrum Kanban
    Rhythm Fixed sprints, usually 1–2 weeks Continuous flow
    Roles Product owner, Scrum master, team None required
    Planning Sprint planning at the start of each sprint Pull new work when capacity frees up
    Key measures Velocity, sprint goal met Cycle time, work in progress
    Best for Feature teams with planned work Operations, bugs, support, mixed work

    Scrum ceremonies: sprint planning · daily standup (15 minutes: done, doing, blocked) · backlog refinement · sprint review and demo · retrospective. Story points measure relative size, not hours.

    Launch checklist:

    Go / no-go: agree the must-pass criteria in advance, and launch only if all of them are met.

    Release notes: lead with the benefit to the user, not the feature name · one line per change · say what users need to do, if anything.

    Retrospectives: what went well, what didn’t, what we’ll change (or Start / Stop / Continue). Every action gets an owner and a date.

    Post-mortems (blameless): timeline · impact on users · root cause found with the 5 Whys · what went well · actions with owners and dates. Focus on fixing the system, not blaming people.

    9. Technical foundations

    You don’t write the code, but you need to know how the pieces fit, so you can reason about cost, speed and risk with engineers.

    Concept What it is Why a PM cares
    Client The app or website the user runs UX and offline behaviour; app-store releases take days to reach users
    Server (backend) Runs the logic and stores the data Where most features, and most cost, live
    API An agreed way for two systems to talk: a request goes in, a response comes back Partner dependencies and rate limits
    REST, webhooks, WebSockets Pull data when asked · get pushed an event · receive a live stream Live prices need streaming; alerts can use webhooks
    Database: SQL or NoSQL Structured tables, or flexible documents Reporting needs; consistency matters when money is involved
    Cache A fast copy of frequently used data Speed, at the risk of showing stale data
    Queue and background jobs Work done later rather than instantly Reliable notifications and reports
    Latency Time taken to respond Traders notice delays in fractions of a second
    Uptime Share of time the system works 99.9% uptime still allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year
    Cloud cost Paying for compute, storage and data transfer Grows with users, and with every AI call
    Security basics Login, encryption, secret keys, least-privilege access Money and personal data are at stake

    How an order flows in India:

    1. The trader places an order in the broker’s app.
    2. The broker’s risk system checks margin and limits.
    3. The order goes to the exchange (NSE or BSE).
    4. The exchange matches it against the order book.
    5. The trade confirmation comes back to the broker and the app.
    6. The clearing corporation settles it: equity delivery settles on T+1, and F&O positions are marked to market daily.
    7. For delivery trades, the depository (NSDL or CDSL) updates the trader’s holdings.

    Questions to ask engineers: What’s the simplest version? What could break? What does it cost per user? How will we know it’s working? What would be hard to undo later?

    10. AI product management

    AI product management is ordinary product management plus one hard fact: the system is probabilistic. You design, measure and ship for it being wrong some of the time.

    How LLMs work, in five ideas:

    1. Tokens: models read and write text in chunks called tokens (in English, roughly 4 characters each). Pricing and limits are counted in tokens.
    2. Context window: the maximum amount of text the model can consider at once, covering your instructions, data and conversation.
    3. Prediction, not knowledge: the model generates likely text. It can sound confident and still be wrong (a hallucination).
    4. Temperature: controls randomness. Use low for consistent answers, higher for creative ones.
    5. No memory by default: each call starts fresh unless you send the history or use a stored memory.
    Approach What it is Use it when Cost and effort
    Prompting Instructions and examples in the request Always try this first Lowest
    RAG (retrieval) Fetch relevant documents and add them to the prompt Answers must use your own or fresh data (news, filings, help docs) and cite sources Medium
    Fine-tuning Train the model further on your examples You need a consistent style or format on a narrow task at scale, and prompting isn’t enough Higher; needs good data
    Agents and tool use The model calls tools (APIs, search, code) over several steps Multi-step tasks; risky actions need human approval Complex and harder to test

    When AI is the wrong answer: a simple rule or formula would work · mistakes are costly and hard to spot · you have no way to evaluate quality · users need an exact answer, such as a margin or tax calculation.

    Evals: how you measure quality

    • Golden dataset: real examples with expected outputs. Start with 30 and grow to 100+.
    • Rubric scoring: accuracy, relevance, groundedness in sources, tone.
    • LLM-as-judge: another model grades outputs against the rubric. Check its grades against your own first.
    • Human review of a sample every week.
    • Regression tests: rerun the evals on every prompt or model change.
    • Live signals: thumbs up or down, edits, and how often users accept the output.
    Failure Example in a trading app Guardrail
    Hallucination Invents a news event or a number RAG with citations; allow “I don’t know”; take numbers from source data, not the model
    Stale information Quotes old prices Fetch live data through tools; show timestamps
    Advice-like output “Buy this option now” Block personalised recommendations; compliance-reviewed wording (in India this touches SEBI’s adviser and research rules)
    Prompt injection A news article contains hidden instructions Treat retrieved text as data only; limit what tools can do
    Inconsistency Different answers to the same question Low temperature; consistency checks in evals
    Privacy leak Shows one user’s data to another Never put other users’ data in a prompt; strict access controls

    AI UX principles: show sources and timestamps · express uncertainty in plain words · make it easy to correct or override · keep a human in the loop for anything that moves money · set expectations (“AI summary; may contain errors”).

    Cost and speed: cost per request is roughly (input tokens + output tokens) × price per token. Cut it with smaller models for simple tasks, caching, shorter prompts and batching. Cut waiting time by streaming responses and precomputing (for example, building summaries before the market opens).

    Metrics for AI features: eval pass rate and groundedness · adoption and repeat use · trust signals (thumbs up, override rate) · cost per active user · response time for the slowest 5% of requests (p95).

    11. Fintech rules for India and Germany

    In fintech, compliance is a product requirement: the rules decide what you can build, say and store. This is a study summary, not legal advice. Check the regulator’s website for the current rules before acting on any of it.

    India: who regulates what

    Body Regulates Why it matters for a fintech product
    SEBI Securities markets: exchanges, brokers, research analysts, investment advisers, algo trading Signals, algos and any advice-like features
    RBI Banks, NBFCs, payments, digital lending Payments, wallets and lending features
    NPCI UPI and other retail payment systems UPI AutoPay for subscriptions
    NSE and BSE Trading, member brokers, algo approvals Algo IDs and API rules
    NSDL and CDSL Holding securities in demat form Holdings data
    AMFI The mutual fund industry body; registers mutual fund distributors Selling, or being paid for, mutual funds
    MeitY and the Data Protection Board Personal data under the DPDP Act Consent, storage and breach reporting

    Rules most relevant to Melange (the first two) and to the trading products you’ll interview for:

    • Investment advice (most important for Melange): SEBI’s Investment Advisers Regulations cover advice about investing in securities, including mutual funds, given for a fee. Melange says it offers general research and is not registered as an investment adviser or research analyst, so the key question is whether a monthly answer ranked for a member’s own amount and years counts as personalised advice. Check the current rules on sebi.gov.in, and get legal advice before charging for the research preview or personalising it further.
    • Selling versus advising: mutual fund distributors, registered with AMFI, earn commission for selling funds. Since 2020 SEBI has required investment advisers to keep advice separate from distribution, so a product that recommends funds and also earns commission on them needs care. (Business Standard)
    • Retail algo trading (SEBI’s 2025 framework): algo orders must go through a broker and carry an exchange-issued algo ID. Algo providers must be empanelled with an exchange. Brokers need controls such as secure API access and a kill switch. Providers of “black box” algos, whose logic isn’t disclosed, must register as SEBI research analysts. (summary)
    • Research and advice: providing buy or sell recommendations or research as a business generally needs SEBI registration as a research analyst or investment adviser. Education and tools that don’t recommend specific trades are treated differently. Get legal advice before launching signals.
    • Finfluencer rules (SEBI, 2024): SEBI-registered firms may not associate with unregistered people who give advice or claim returns. This affects marketing and partnerships.
    • F&O risk measures: from late 2024, SEBI raised minimum contract sizes for index derivatives, limited weekly expiries, and required option premiums to be collected upfront. Check the current rules before designing expiry-day features.
    • KYC and anti-money-laundering: brokers must verify identity (often through CKYC and video KYC) and monitor suspicious activity under the PMLA.
    • DPDP Act 2023 and DPDP Rules 2025: the Rules were notified on Nov 13, 2025. Most company obligations (notices, consent, security safeguards, breach reporting, user rights) apply from May 13, 2027. Breaches must be reported to the Data Protection Board without delay, with a detailed report within 72 hours. (summary)

    Germany and the EU

    Rule or body What it covers What it means for a product
    BaFin Germany’s financial regulator for banks, brokers, payment and investment firms Licences and conduct rules
    MiFID II EU rules for investment services Suitability and appropriateness checks, best execution, cost disclosure, record-keeping
    PSD2 Payment services and open banking Strong customer authentication; account access through APIs
    GDPR Personal data Lawful basis, consent, user rights, breach notice within 72 hours
    EU AI Act AI systems, by risk level Credit scoring counts as high-risk; chatbots must disclose they’re AI; obligations phase in through 2026–27
    DORA Digital resilience of financial firms (in force since January 2025) Incident reporting, resilience testing, managing cloud and AI vendor risk

    Compliance as a PM habit: involve compliance during discovery, not the week before launch · give every PRD a “regulatory impact” section · avoid words like “guaranteed”, “safe” or “assured returns” · keep audit trails · never give personalised recommendations without the right licence.

    12. Stakeholders and communication

    PMs lead without authority, so clear writing and earned trust are their main tools.

    Stakeholder map (power × interest):

    Low interest High interest
    High power Keep satisfied: short updates, no surprises Manage closely: involve them in decisions
    Low power Monitor: occasional updates Keep informed: regular updates, ask for input

    RACI: for each piece of work, name who is Responsible (does it), who is Accountable (one person owns the outcome), who is Consulted (gives input before) and who is Informed (told after). For a Melange launch, you are R and A; a compliance adviser and three research-preview members are C; all users are I.

    Writing:

    • Answer first (the pyramid principle): conclusion, then 3 supporting points, then details.
    • One-pager: problem · proposal · why now · cost · risks · the decision needed, and by when.
    • Weekly update: progress against the goal in numbers · what shipped · what’s next · risks and asks.
    • Decision memo: context · options · recommendation · trade-offs · decision and owner.

    Templates for all of these are in the Templates tab.

    Meetings: every meeting needs a purpose, an owner and an output (a decision, a plan or a list of actions). Send the agenda before and the notes after: decisions, owners, dates.

    Conflict and influence:

    • Disagree with data, not opinions, and separate the person from the problem.
    • Find the goal you share, then argue about the path.
    • Once a decision is made, “disagree and commit”.
    • Escalate early, bringing options rather than complaints.
    • Saying no to a senior person: “We can do X by [date] if we drop Y. Which matters more?”

    13. Interviews: model answers

    These model answers show the structure and depth interviewers look for. Replace every [bracket] with your own facts, and never claim anything you can’t back up. The answer structure for each round is in the 4-week interview sprint tab of the program doc.

    Tell me about yourself (90 seconds)

    I’m a full-time F&O trader, and for [X] years I’ve made decisions under risk every day, with my own capital at stake. I built my own trading platform, which checks each trade against market conditions and behavioural rules. Then I built Melange Research for people who invest through monthly SIPs: free charts of the economy and markets, and for members, one plain-language answer each month on whether that month’s money goes into shares, gold or a mix, tested on past Indian data after costs and tax. I built it because [why you started Melange]. Building it, I found that [what you enjoyed most: talking to investors, deciding what to build, measuring whether it worked]. Now I want to do that full time in a product team, and [company] is where my domain knowledge counts most, because [a specific reason about their product or users].

    “You have no PM experience. Why should we hire you?”

    That’s fair: I haven’t held the title. But I’ve done the core of the job. I found a problem SIP investors have, built Melange Research to solve it, spoke to [N] investors to test it, and made trade-offs about what to build first. As a trader I make decisions with incomplete data and measure the results every day, which is most of a PM’s job. I’ve also worked through a structured PM program, and I can show you my graded work: [portfolio link].

    The pattern: acknowledge the gap, reframe it with evidence, and show proof of learning.

    Product sense: “Design a product for first-time F&O traders”

    1. Clarify: the goal is to help new traders trade more safely and stay; mobile first; India.
    2. Segment: young earners and students trying options with small capital · experienced equity investors moving into F&O · people following tips. Pick the first: the largest group and the most at risk.
    3. Pain points: they don’t understand leverage and margin · they lose money fast on expiry days · they trade without a plan · nothing tells them what went wrong.
    4. Prioritise: losing money fast without understanding why. It’s the biggest pain and a regulatory concern, since SEBI’s studies have found that most individual F&O traders lose money.
    5. Three solutions: a paper-trading mode for the first two weeks · a pre-trade preview of the maximum loss in rupees and as a share of capital · a post-trade review that explains what happened.
    6. Pick the maximum-loss preview: it’s the smallest build and acts at the moment of decision. The trade-off: some users will find it annoying, so let them collapse it after 10 trades.
    7. Success metrics: north star: new traders still active after 60 days whose losses stayed under 20% of their capital. Inputs: previews viewed, orders changed after a preview. Guardrails: time to place an order, complaints.
    8. Risks: users ignore it, and the wording must not read as advice.

    Metric drop: “Daily trades fell 20% this week”

    First I’d clarify: all users or some, and did it drop suddenly on a particular day? Then I’d rule out a tracking problem. Next, internal causes: did we ship a release, change pricing, or have an outage or login bug? Then external ones: a market holiday, low volatility, an expiry-rule change, or a competitor offer. Then I’d segment. If the drop is only on the latest Android version, it’s probably a bug in that release. Finally I’d find the funnel step: if logins are normal but orders placed are down, the order screen is the suspect. I’d confirm with data, fix it, and add an alert.

    Strategy: “Should a large discount broker build an AI research assistant?”

    I’d start with the broker’s goals: keep active traders, cut support load, and protect its reputation for trust. Its strengths are a large active user base and a library of education content. The risks are advice regulation, AI errors where money is involved, and cost. The options: (a) AI answers drawn from its own help and education content, which is low risk; (b) AI summaries of news and company filings, with citations; (c) personalised trade ideas, which carry high regulatory risk. I’d recommend (a), then (b), and not (c). I’d test (a) with 1% of users and measure support tickets avoided, answer accuracy in evals, and user trust.

    Behavioural (STAR): “Tell me about a decision you made with incomplete information”

    Situation: during [a volatile market event], a position moved sharply against me before key data was out. Task: decide whether to exit or hold, with limited information. Action: I separated what I knew from what I was assuming, set the maximum loss I would accept, exited half to cut my risk, and set an alert for the data release. Result: I limited the loss to [X]%, against [Y]% if I had held. Learning: I now set exit rules before entering a trade, and that idea became one of the checks in my trading platform.

    AI PM: “How would you add AI to a broker app?”

    I’d start from a user problem, not from AI: for example, new traders don’t understand why a position is losing money. Is AI the right tool? Partly. The numbers must come from deterministic calculations, while AI explains them in plain language. The data needed is positions, prices and the user’s margin. The approach is prompting plus retrieval from the broker’s own education content, with no fine-tuning at first. Evals: 50 real questions with expert answers, scored for accuracy and for not crossing into advice. Guardrails: no buy or sell recommendations, show the source for every number, allow “I don’t know”. Success: fewer support tickets on the topic, plus a trust rating; guardrails on cost per user and response time.

    Metrics and goals: “Set the north-star metric for a broker app”

    I’d start from the value users get. For a broker, that’s investing and trading with confidence, so revenue and downloads are results, not the value itself. My north star would be monthly active investors who place at least one order. Inputs: new accounts that finish KYC and add money, a first order within 7 days, SIPs started, and repeat orders per active user. Guardrails: failed or rejected orders, complaints, and the share of F&O users losing most of their capital, so growth never comes from harmful overtrading. I’d check that the team can move it within weeks, and agree it with leadership before setting targets.

    Estimation

    The worked examples are in Lesson 2: Quicko users who hit the manual-section problem, and Kite’s daily users. Out loud, it sounds like this:

    Let me check the scope first: India, this year, people rather than accounts? I’ll go top-down from [a population you know], because [reason]. My assumptions are [each with a one-line reason]. That gives about [result]. As a sanity check, [a second way to get there] lands in the same range, so I’m comfortable with roughly [result].

    Execution and trade-offs: “Your launch is two weeks late. What do you do?”

    First I’d find out why it slipped and how firm the new date is: one blocked task, or estimates that were wrong across the board? Then I’d lay out the options: cut scope and ship the most valuable part on time, move the date, or add people, which rarely helps late in a project. I’d choose based on why the date matters. If it’s a regulatory deadline or a public commitment, I’d cut scope; if quality matters more, I’d move the date. I’d tell stakeholders early with the options and my recommendation, and run a short retro afterwards on why the estimate was off.

    Recruiter screen: “Why are you moving into product?”

    Trading taught me to make decisions with incomplete information and to measure every result. Building my trading platform and Melange Research showed me that what I enjoy most is [understanding users, deciding what to build, seeing whether it worked]. I want to do that full time, in a team, for many more users. [Company] stands out to me because [a specific reason]. I can start within [X] weeks, and my expected range is [a range you’ve researched].

    Fintech twist (any round)

    Add a short risk-and-trust step to any answer:

    Because this involves people’s money, I’d also check three things: which SEBI or RBI rules apply, for example whether this counts as investment advice; how we prevent fraud and costly errors; and how we keep users’ trust if something goes wrong, with clear disclosures and an easy way to reach support.

    Take-home assignment

    Lead with your recommendation, then follow the one-page structure: problem and user → evidence → 2–3 options → recommendation → metrics → risks → next steps. State your assumptions, stay within the time limit, and end with what you’d do with more time. Interviewers grade clarity and judgment, not length.

    Questions to ask interviewers

    • What problem would I own in my first 90 days?
    • How do you decide what goes on the roadmap?
    • How do PMs work with compliance here?
    • What would success look like in this role after a year?
    • How do you measure the quality of your AI features?
    • What’s the biggest product bet the team is making this year?

    Salary and notice period

    Research the salary range for the role first. Give a range whose bottom is your real target, and avoid naming numbers until you understand the role. For Germany, ask about relocation and visa support early.

    Common mistakes

    Jumping to solutions · no metrics · rambling without structure · not asking clarifying questions · criticising past employers or competitors · not having used the company’s product before the interview.

    14. Mutual funds and SIPs in India

    This is Melange’s world. You need it to talk to members, size the market, judge competitors and answer fintech interview questions. Figures change, so check the sources before quoting them.

    How a mutual fund works: investors pool money, a fund house (AMC) invests it, and each investor holds units. The price of one unit, the NAV, is worked out each business day. SEBI regulates mutual funds; AMFI is the industry body that registers distributors and publishes industry data.

    How a SIP works: a fixed amount moves from the investor’s bank account on a set date each month, through a bank mandate (NACH or UPI AutoPay), and buys units at that day’s NAV. Buying every month means buying more units when prices are low and fewer when they’re high. Investors can step a SIP up, pause it or stop it, and stopping after a fall is exactly the behaviour Melange’s research is meant to prevent.

    The market (AMFI, August 2026): 10.02 crore contributing SIP accounts, ₹32,297 crore invested through SIPs that month, and SIP assets of ₹18.62 lakh crore, about 21.4% of the industry’s ₹87.08 lakh crore. (source) AMFI also reports SIPs stopped against SIPs started each month, a useful signal for Melange’s counter-metric.

    Direct and regular plans: every fund has both. They hold the same investments, but a regular plan pays a distributor’s commission out of a higher expense ratio, so it costs the investor more every year. Direct plans have existed since 2013.

    Costs:

    • Expense ratio (TER): the yearly fee, taken out of the NAV daily. SEBI caps it, with lower caps for larger funds.
    • Exit load: a charge for leaving within a set period, often a year for equity funds.

    Categories: SEBI groups funds into equity (large, mid and small cap, flexi-cap, sector funds, ELSS for tax saving), debt, hybrid, index funds and ETFs, and others such as gold funds and funds of funds. Each fund must stick to its category’s rules, which makes comparisons fairer.

    Tax on gains (rules for FY 2025-26; check for later years): (source)

    Investment Short term Long term
    Equity funds 12 months or less: 20% Over 12 months: 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year
    Debt funds bought from April 1, 2023 Taxed at the investor’s slab rate, however long they’re held
    Gold ETFs 12 months or less Over 12 months, as listed securities
    Gold mutual funds Rules depend on the purchase date; check before saying anything about them
    Sovereign Gold Bonds Interest of 2.5% a year is taxed at the slab rate Gains at maturity are tax-free

    Who may advise and who may sell:

    Who Registered with Paid by What it means for Melange
    Investment adviser SEBI Fees from the client May give personalised advice
    Research analyst SEBI Fees for research May publish research and recommendations on securities
    Mutual fund distributor AMFI Commission from fund houses Sells regular plans
    Direct-plan platforms (for example Zerodha Coin, Groww, Kuvera) Through their licences Their own business models Where many of Melange’s members already invest

    Questions to explore with members: how they chose their funds, how they split money between shares and gold, what they did in the last market fall, and whom they trust for advice today.

    15. Getting hired in India, Europe, Singapore and Canada

    Your search runs in four regions with different habits. Check visa rules on official sites before acting; they change every year.

    India

    • Where roles appear: LinkedIn, company career pages, Instahyre, Wellfound (startups), Cutshort and Naukri. Fintech PM roles often go to referrals first, so message PMs at your target companies.
    • Resume: one page, impact bullets, no photo. Put Melange and your portfolio link near the top.
    • Notice period: employers ask early, and 30 to 90 days is common. As a self-employed trader you can join quickly, which is a real advantage, so say so.
    • Salary research: AmbitionBox, Glassdoor and conversations with recruiters. Let them name a range first when you can.

    Germany

    • Where roles appear: LinkedIn, StepStone, Berlin Startup Jobs and company career pages. Fintechs such as Trade Republic, Scalable Capital, N26, Raisin, Solaris and Upvest often work in English.
    • CV (Lebenslauf): one to two pages, newest first, with month and year for every role. A photo is optional. A tailored one-page cover letter (Anschreiben) is often expected, and reference letters from past employers carry weight.
    • EU Blue Card (2026): a job offer paying at least €50,700 gross a year, or €45,934.20 in shortage occupations such as IT, plus a degree recognised in Germany. IT specialists without a degree can qualify with three years of IT experience in the last seven. Ask employers whether a PM role counts as IT for this. (source)
    • Opportunity Card (Chancenkarte): up to 12 months in Germany to look for work. You qualify through full recognition of your qualification or with 6 points (for qualification, experience, language and age), and you need proof of €1,091 a month for 2026. You may work part-time, up to 20 hours a week, while you search. (source)
    • Language: many fintech teams work in English, but German at A1 to B1 helps in daily life, widens your options and earns Opportunity Card points.
    • Timeline: visa processing can take weeks to months, so agree start dates with that in mind, and ask about relocation support.
    • Salary: quoted as gross per year. Research on Glassdoor and levels.fyi before any conversation.

    Elsewhere in Europe

    • Where roles appear: LinkedIn, Welcome to the Jungle (formerly Otta) and company career pages. Investing and fintech firms hiring PMs include Revolut, Monzo, Wise, Bitpanda, Trading 212, eToro, N26, Raisin, bunq and Adyen.
    • United Kingdom: a Skilled Worker visa needs an employer licensed to sponsor you and, in general, a salary of at least £41,700 a year (since July 2025). Check gov.uk for your role’s going rate. (source)
    • Netherlands: the highly skilled migrant route needs a recognised sponsor and, from January 1, 2026, at least €5,942 gross a month at age 30 or older (€4,357 under 30), excluding holiday allowance. (source)
    • Other EU countries (Ireland, France, Spain, Lithuania and more) run the EU Blue Card with their own salary thresholds, so check each country’s official site.

    Singapore

    • Where roles appear: LinkedIn, MyCareersFuture (the government job portal), NodeFlair and company career pages. Wealth and investing firms include Endowus, StashAway, Syfe, moomoo and Tiger Brokers, alongside banks, payment firms and crypto exchanges.
    • Employment Pass: your employer applies, not you. For new applications before January 1, 2027, the minimum monthly salary is S$5,600 in most sectors and S$6,200 in financial services at age 23, rising with age: about S$7,223 and S$7,982 at 30, and up to S$10,700 and S$11,800 at 45 and above. From January 1, 2027 the starting figures rise to S$6,000 and S$6,600. The application must also score 40 points under COMPASS. (source)
    • Hiring timeline: many employers must advertise a role on MyCareersFuture before applying for an Employment Pass, which can add a couple of weeks. Ask early whether they sponsor.

    Canada

    • Where roles appear: LinkedIn, Job Bank (the government portal), Indeed and company career pages. Toronto is the main fintech hub. Investing and trading firms include Wealthsimple, Questrade, Qtrade, TMX Group and the direct-investing arms of the big banks, alongside crypto platforms such as Coinsquare, Newton and Shakepay.
    • Working there: most foreign workers need an employer-backed work permit. Under the Global Talent Stream, the government aims to process the employer’s labour market assessment in about 10 business days. Its fast-track occupation list includes computer and information systems managers but doesn’t name product managers, so ask the employer how they’d classify the role. (source)
    • Permanent residence: Express Entry ranks candidates by points. Job offers stopped earning points in March 2025, and a 2026 consultation proposed bringing them back only for high-wage jobs, so check the current rules on canada.ca. (source)

    All markets: check visa rules on official sites: Make it in Germany, gov.uk, Singapore’s Ministry of Manpower (mom.gov.sg) and canada.ca. The hub’s Jobs page lists current openings by region. Track every application in the hub, follow up once after 5 to 7 days, and read your funnel every Sunday (Lesson 15).

    16. Trading and markets roles where your experience is the edge

    Product roles are your main goal, but some roles hire mainly for what you already have: live F&O trading, risk discipline and a feel for how markets behave. The hub’s Jobs page lists them as group 6. Apply to the ones that fit alongside your product applications. They are also a way into a broker or exchange, and into a product role from there.

    Roles to look for:

    Role What they want Your edge
    Dealer or execution trader at a broker Fast, accurate order handling, exchange rules, calm under pressure You place and manage derivatives orders every day
    Trader at a crypto exchange, market maker or prop desk Options and futures pricing, risk limits, markets that never close Options pricing, the Greeks and position sizing are your daily tools
    Risk, margin and RMS analyst Margin rules, exposure and position limits, stress scenarios You manage margin and drawdowns on your own book
    Trade surveillance analyst Spotting manipulation and unusual activity, exchange rules You know what real order flow and abuse look like
    Product specialist for options, derivatives or trading tools Explaining products to clients and to product teams It leads straight into product management
    Research analyst, market content and investor education Clear market writing and analysis Melange Research is your portfolio
    Trading or market operations Order lifecycle, settlement, corporate actions You know the trade lifecycle from the user’s side

    Licences by region:

    • India: dealers and sales staff in equity derivatives at a broker need NISM Series VIII (Equity Derivatives), the exam NISM describes as meant for “approved users and sales personnel of the trading member”. Research analysts need NISM Series XV, valid for three years, and a degree in a relevant field such as finance or economics. (NISM, NISM)
    • Singapore: client-facing representatives in capital markets must pass CMFAS exams run by the Institute of Banking and Finance: Rules, Ethics and Skills modules plus a product module, in the structure in force since April 1, 2024. Internal risk, surveillance and operations roles usually don’t need them. (source)
    • Canada: since January 1, 2026, new candidates at dealers regulated by CIRO take the Canadian Investment Regulatory Exam (CIRE) instead of the Canadian Securities Course. Roles that advise clients also need the Retail Securities Exam. (source)
    • Europe: trading, risk and surveillance roles rarely ask for an exam before hiring; firms train and certify new staff themselves.

    How to pitch it:

    • Lead with process, not profit: instruments, years traded, position sizing, risk rules, maximum drawdown and how you review trades. Firms are wary of traders who chase P&L.
    • Bring one page of evidence: a summary of your trading journal, your risk rules, and one trade you got wrong and what you changed after it.
    • For product specialist and research roles, show your trading platform and Melange Research.
    • Elite trading firms such as Optiver, Jane Street and IMC mostly hire experienced traders from other desks, or graduates through tests. The hub marks them “Long shot”. Put your effort into brokers, exchanges and crypto venues first.
    • Each week, also check eFinancialCareers and a LinkedIn search for derivatives and trading roles in your regions. Both are linked on the hub’s Jobs page.

    17. Open-door roles where your skills transfer

    Some roles at your target companies hire on skills rather than a set degree or job title. They often pay less than product roles at first, but they put you inside a broker, exchange or fintech, and moving into product from inside is far easier than applying from outside. The hub’s Jobs page lists them as group 7.

    Roles to look for:

    Role What they want What you can show
    Business or functional analyst for capital markets and trading systems Turning business needs into clear requirements, domain knowledge You know orders, margin and settlement first-hand, and you’ve designed a trading platform
    Data or business analyst SQL, spreadsheets, dashboards, clear findings Your trading journal and the analysis behind Melange Research
    Business operations, or strategy and operations Structured problem solving, running processes You run a trading business: risk rules, records and accounts
    Customer success, onboarding and implementation Helping clients get value from a product, often a technical one You use trading tools and APIs every day and can explain them
    Community, content and education Clear writing and a portfolio Melange Research and your posts
    Testing for trading apps (user acceptance or functional testing) Careful testing against real user flows You know the edge cases a trader actually hits
    Project or program coordinator Plans, follow-ups, stakeholder updates The program and tracker you’re running now

    How to apply:

    • Read the requirements as a list of skills, not a filter. If you meet most of them and can show proof, apply. Many of these listings accept any degree.
    • Put proof at the top of your resume: the trading platform, Melange Research, your trading journal and the product work from this program.
    • Expect a short test: SQL or spreadsheet tasks for analyst roles, a writing sample for content roles, a role play for customer success.
    • Once inside, tell your manager you want to move into product, and volunteer for product work such as user research, writing specs and analysing launches. Many companies let you apply for internal roles after about a year.

    Question bank

    Questions for each day’s drill, so you can practise with or without an AI tool. Pick one you haven’t done, set a timer, answer out loud using the answer structure for that round (in the 4-week interview sprint tab), then compare with the outline and self-grade with the rubric. Mark each question with the date you did it and your score.

    How to use it

    • Drill block (30 minutes): one question, 20 minutes to answer, 10 to compare and score.
    • Without AI: answer on paper, then check your answer against the outline and the model answers in cheat sheet 13.
    • With AI: paste the question into the Drill prompt instead of letting the AI choose.
    • Repeat your weakest type: your scorecard shows which round needs the most work.

    Guesstimates

    # Question Outline
    G1 How many people in India start a new SIP in a month? Start from AMFI’s new SIP registrations, or top-down: investors × share starting one in a month; check against monthly SIP account growth
    G2 How many people use Zerodha Kite on a typical trading day? Worked in Lesson 2: split active traders and investors by how often they open the app
    G3 How much money do Indians invest through SIPs in a year? Monthly SIP inflow × 12 (AMFI publishes it monthly); sanity-check against accounts × average ticket size
    G4 How many UPI payments are made in India each day? Users × payments per user per day by segment; check against NPCI’s monthly figures ÷ 30
    G5 How many people in Bengaluru would pay for a personal finance course? Adults → working professionals → those who invest → those willing to pay for learning → a realistic share
    G6 How many support tickets would a broker with 50 lakh active clients get on an expiry day? Active that day × share who hit a problem × share who contact support; segment by issue type
    G7 What’s the market size for a paid research subscription for SIP investors in India? Investors → those choosing their own funds → those who pay for research → price per year
    G8 How many ITR-3 filers use an online tax tool? Taxpayers filing ITR-3 → share self-filing → share using a tool (Lesson 2 shows a similar chain)
    G9 How many credit cards are swiped in India on Diwali day? Cards in use × share used that day × transactions per card; compare with an ordinary day
    G10 How many people in Germany use a neobank as their main account? Adults → have a smartphone bank → neobank as main account; state each share with a reason

    Product sense

    # Question Outline
    P1 Design a product for first-time F&O traders. Model answer in cheat sheet 13
    P2 Improve Melange for someone who has just started their first SIP. Segment new SIP investors; pain is fear and confusion; first answer, explanations, small wins; metric: still investing at 6 months
    P3 How would you improve Groww’s or Zerodha Coin’s mutual fund experience? Pick one segment, one pain (choosing funds, tracking goals), three solutions, pick one with a trade-off
    P4 Design a product that helps Indian families plan for a child’s education. Segment by child’s age and income; pain is not knowing how much and where; goal calculator plus a monthly nudge
    P5 What’s your favourite fintech product, and how would you improve it? Say why it’s great (a specific job done well), then one improvement for one segment, with a metric
    P6 Design a feature to stop users panic-selling during a market fall. Users who sell at lows; show history of past falls and recoveries; friction before selling; guardrail: don’t block legitimate needs
    P7 Design a product for gig workers to save regularly. Irregular income is the core pain; save a share of each payout; UPI AutoPay; metric: months with savings
    P8 How would you help Indians living in Germany invest back home? Segment by visa and tax status; pains: KYC, tax in two countries, transfers; start with information and a checklist
    P9 Design a product to help senior citizens avoid investment fraud. Fraud patterns, trusted contacts, verification of advisers; trust and accessibility matter most
    P10 What would you build next for melangeresearch.com, and why? Use your insight report: biggest pain × frequency; one bet with a cheap test and a success metric

    Metrics and diagnosis

    # Question Outline
    M1 Set the north-star metric for a broker app. Model answer in cheat sheet 13
    M2 Melange’s monthly answer reads fell 30% this month. What do you do? Is it real? → when did it start? → internal (email, release, data delay) vs external (market, holiday) → segment → funnel step
    M3 A broker’s daily trades fell 20% this week. Diagnose it. Model answer in cheat sheet 13
    M4 SIP cancellations doubled last month on an investing app. Why? Market fall, bank mandate failures, app change, a competitor offer; segment by tenure and fund type
    M5 How would you measure the success of a UPI app’s “split the bill” feature? Goal → north star (bills settled) → inputs (splits created, friends invited) → guardrails (failed payments, complaints)
    M6 Sign-ups are up 40% but revenue is flat. What’s going on? Mix of users changed, activation fell, trial users not converting, pricing change; segment by source
    M7 Define success for an AI customer-support assistant at a bank. Resolution without a human, accuracy in evals, customer satisfaction; guardrails: wrong answers about money, escalation time
    M8 Which metrics would you put on Melange’s weekly dashboard? North star, 3 inputs, 2 guardrails, one counter-metric; each with an owner and a target

    Execution and trade-offs

    # Question Outline
    E1 Your launch is two weeks late. What do you do? Model answer in cheat sheet 13
    E2 How would you launch a new mutual fund screener? Goal and metric → smallest version → rollout stages → kill switch → support briefing → review at 1 and 4 weeks
    E3 Engineering wants a month for tech debt; sales wants a feature. How do you decide? Cost of each delay, risk if debt isn’t fixed, split capacity, agree a rule (for example 20% for debt)
    E4 A bug shows some users the wrong portfolio value. What do you do in the first hour? Contain (turn off, banner), size the impact, communicate, fix, then a blameless post-mortem
    E5 You can build only one of two features this quarter. How do you choose? Goal, evidence for each, RICE, cost of delay, reversibility; decide and write down why
    E6 Compliance blocks your launch two days before release. What now? Understand the exact concern, options (change wording, narrow the audience, delay), agree a path, update stakeholders
    E7 How would you prioritise 50 feature requests from users? Group by underlying problem, size each problem, check against strategy, say no with reasons
    E8 Your experiment shows a 5% lift, but only on Android. Do you ship? Check sample size and novelty, look for a bug, ship to Android with monitoring, investigate iOS

    Strategy

    # Question Outline
    S1 Should a large discount broker build an AI research assistant? Model answer in cheat sheet 13
    S2 Should Melange charge for its research preview now? Evidence of repeat value first; compliance question; options and a cheap pricing test
    S3 How should an Indian investing app enter Germany? Different regulation, customer and competitors; start with the Indian diaspora or partner with a licensed firm
    S4 A competitor launches free advisory. How do you respond? Don’t copy blindly; check what your users value; strengthen your differentiator; watch churn
    S5 Should a payments company start offering loans? Data advantage, regulation (RBI), credit risk, capital needs; start narrow with a partner
    S6 What’s the biggest opportunity in Indian wealth-tech in the next 3 years? Pick one trend (SIP growth, smaller cities, AI advice), size it, name the risks

    AI product management

    # Question Outline
    A1 How would you add AI to a broker app? Model answer in cheat sheet 13
    A2 Should Melange use AI to write its monthly answer? AI explains, the research model decides; risks (hallucination, advice); evals and human review
    A3 How would you evaluate an AI that summarises company results for investors? Golden set of filings, key facts per summary, accuracy and grounding scores, LLM-as-judge checked by people
    A4 Your AI chatbot gave a user wrong tax information. What do you do? Contain, check how often it happens, fix with RAG and refusal rules, add the case to evals, tell affected users
    A5 When should you not use AI in a fintech product? A rule or formula works; mistakes are costly and hard to spot; you can’t evaluate quality; exact numbers needed
    A6 How would you cut the cost of an AI feature by half? Smaller model where evals allow, shorter prompts, caching, batching, precomputing
    A7 Design an AI assistant for mutual fund distributors. Their job: explain funds and paperwork to clients; data from fund documents; compliance guardrails; time saved as the metric
    A8 How do you build user trust in an AI feature? Show sources, admit uncertainty, easy correction, human in the loop for money decisions, consistent answers

    Behavioural

    # Question Outline
    B1 Tell me about yourself. Model answer in cheat sheet 13
    B2 Tell me about a decision you made with incomplete information. Model answer in cheat sheet 13
    B3 Tell me about a time you failed. A real failure, your part in it, what you changed afterwards; no fake failures
    B4 Tell me about something you built from scratch. Melange: the problem, the users, your key decisions and trade-offs, the result
    B5 Tell me about a time you changed your mind because of data. A belief, the evidence, what you did differently, the outcome
    B6 Tell me about a disagreement and how you handled it. Shared goal, data over opinion, the resolution, the relationship afterwards
    B7 How did you persuade someone without authority? Their incentives, your evidence, a small first step, the result
    B8 Tell me about a time you learned a new skill fast. PM itself: how you structured the learning, what you produced, how you checked quality
    B9 Why are you moving from trading into product? Model answer in cheat sheet 13 (recruiter screen)
    B10 Describe a time you handled pressure or a loss. A trading drawdown: your process, the decision, the lesson, the rule you made

    Fintech

    # Question Outline
    F1 What’s the difference between an investment adviser and a mutual fund distributor in India? Adviser: SEBI-registered, paid fees by the client; distributor: AMFI-registered, paid commission; cheat sheet 14
    F2 How would you design KYC onboarding that’s fast and compliant? Digital KYC, CKYC reuse, clear steps, drop-off tracking, fraud checks
    F3 What does the DPDP Act mean for a fintech product team? Consent, purpose, minimal data, user rights, breach reporting; most duties from May 2027
    F4 How would a German neobank differ from an Indian one? Regulation (BaFin, PSD2), payment habits (cards and SEPA vs UPI), privacy expectations (GDPR)
    F5 Why do most retail F&O traders lose money, and what should a broker do about it? SEBI’s studies; leverage and overtrading; education, risk previews and friction; regulatory pressure
    F6 How would you explain direct and regular mutual fund plans to a new investor? Same fund, different cost: regular plans pay a distributor commission through a higher expense ratio; cheat sheet 14

    Interview request (WhatsApp, LinkedIn or email)

    Hi [name], I'm [your name]. I'm researching how people who invest through monthly SIPs decide where their money goes, for a product I'm building called Melange Research.

Could I ask you about your own experience for 20-30 minutes, on a call this week? I'm not selling anything, and there are no right answers. I'll share a short summary of what I learn as a thank-you.

Does [day] at [time] work, or is another time better?

    Send about 8 requests for every 3 interviews you need, and follow up once after 3 days.

    Interview consent script (read at the start)

    Thanks for your time. I'm learning how people manage their SIPs, not testing you or selling anything.
- It will take about 30 minutes, and you can skip any question.
- Is it OK if I take notes? I won't use your name, and I won't ask for account numbers or amounts unless you want to share them.
- I may quote what you say, without your name, in my own notes and product work.
Shall we start?

    User interview guide (30 minutes)

    INTERVIEW GUIDE: [topic]
Date: [ ]   Participant: [segment, not their name]
What I need to learn: [ ]

1. Intro and consent (2 min): "I'm learning how people who invest through SIPs handle [topic]. There are no right answers. Is it OK if I take notes?"
2. Context (5 min): "Tell me about your investing. What do you put money into each month, how did you choose it, and which apps do you use?"
3. The last time (15 min): "Tell me about the last time [problem] happened."
   What happened just before? What did you do? How did it end? What did it cost you?
4. Workarounds (5 min): "What do you do about this today? What have you tried or paid for?"
5. Wrap-up (3 min): "Is there anything I should have asked? Who else should I talk to?"

Never ask: "Would you use...?", "Would you pay...?", "Do you like my idea?"
